items.title: Google DeepMind integrates computer use into Gemini 3.5 Flash to enable cross-platform agent interactions and improve enterprise automation tasks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Introducing computer use in Gemini 3.5 Flash
items.summary:
Google DeepMind has integrated computer use capabilities directly into its Gemini 3.5 Flash model, enhancing its ability to build agents that interact seamlessly across browser, mobile, and desktop platforms. This integration improves performance on complex, long-term tasks such as continuous software testing and enterprise automation, allowing agents to see, reason, and act within various professional applications.

Previously available only as a standalone model, computer use is now a native feature of Gemini 3.5 Flash, accessible through the Gemini API and Enterprise Agent Platform. To address security concerns, DeepMind has implemented targeted adversarial training and introduced enterprise safeguards that require user confirmation for sensitive actions and can halt tasks if prompt injection is detected. These measures, combined with recommended best practices like sandboxing and human oversight, aim to ensure safe deployment in live environments.

items.title: OpenAI unveils Jalapeño, its first custom inference chip built by Broadcom, designed to optimize AI model performance and efficiency [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenAI unveils its first custom chip, built by Broadcom
items.summary:
OpenAI has introduced Jalapeño, its first custom inference chip developed in partnership with Broadcom to enhance the performance and efficiency of its AI models. The chip is tailored specifically for OpenAI's inference workloads, aiming to deliver better performance-per-watt compared to existing solutions. This move reflects OpenAI's strategy to optimize its AI infrastructure by designing hardware that complements its software and operational needs.

Jalapeño focuses on accelerating inference tasks, which involve running pre-trained AI models in response to user inputs, and is expected to reduce operating costs, particularly for real-time applications like coding models. While more demanding processes such as model pre-training may continue to rely on Nvidia GPUs, this chip represents a significant step in OpenAI's efforts to control costs and improve efficiency across its AI stack by integrating custom hardware, software, and data center design.

items.title: RubyLLM launches a unified Ruby framework supporting all major AI providers with features for chatbots, AI agents, image generation, transcription, and more [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: RubyLLM: A Ruby framework for all major AI providers
items.summary:
RubyLLM has introduced a unified Ruby framework that supports all major AI providers, enabling developers to build chatbots, AI agents, image generation tools, transcription services, and various AI workflows with a consistent interface. The framework simplifies integration by providing a single API for multiple AI models, including GPT, Claude, and local options like Ollama, reducing the complexity of managing different APIs and response formats.

The framework offers features such as conversational AI, image and video analysis, audio transcription, document extraction, image generation, embeddings, content moderation, and tool integration for custom Ruby methods. It also supports structured JSON output, real-time streaming responses, Rails integration, asynchronous concurrency, and access to over 800 AI models from providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google VertexAI. RubyLLM aims to streamline AI development in Ruby with minimal dependencies and easy installation.

items.title: Researchers present Sol Video Inference Engine, an agent-native acceleration framework that doubles video diffusion model inference speed with minimal quality loss across diverse models and hardware [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Sol Video Inference Engine: Agent-Native Full-Stack Acceleration Framework for Efficient Video Generation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed the Sol Video Inference Engine, a training-free acceleration framework designed to enhance the efficiency of video diffusion models. This framework integrates five optimization techniques—cache, sparse attention, token pruning, quantization, and kernel fusion—into an agent-based system that tailors acceleration strategies to specific combinations of models, hardware, and inference settings. By automating the tuning process with parallel skill agents and human validation, Sol achieves over twice the inference speed while maintaining near-original video quality across diverse video models and hardware platforms.

The framework addresses the challenge that acceleration methods often do not generalize well due to variations in model architectures, numerical sensitivities, and hardware capabilities. It was tested on three different video diffusion models of varying sizes and architectures, demonstrating significant speed improvements with minimal quality loss. This approach reduces the need for costly manual performance engineering and offers a scalable solution for efficient video generation in various deployment scenarios.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.23743v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern video diffusion models achieve higher generation quality through scaling, but this also increases inference cost. Although many acceleration methods have been proposed, a central challenge is that the most effective acceleration strategy is highly instance-specific: a recipe that works well for one combination of model, hardware, and inference configuration often does not transfer to another. Different models vary in architecture, numerical sensitivity, and attention concentration patterns. Inference settings differ in spatial and temporal resolution and video duration, while hardware platforms differ in memory hierarchy, supported numerical formats, and kernel throughput. These factors create a large tuning space, making manual performance engineering costly. We present Sol Video Inference Engine, an agentic, native, training-free acceleration framework for video diffusion models. It organizes five broadly applicable techniques, cache, sparse attention, token pruning, quantization, and kernel fusion, into an agentic acceleration stack for instance-specific optimization. For a concrete deployment target defined by a model, hardware platform, and serving configuration, parallel skill agents optimize the implementation of each technique, an agent integrator composes them into a global acceleration stack, and a human validator provides feedback on generation quality. We instantiate this workflow on three video models with different sizes and architectures: 64B Cosmos3-Super, 22B LTX-2.3, and 2B SANA-Video. With little human effort, the full stack achieves more than 2x end-to-end acceleration while maintaining near-lossless VBench quality, demonstrating the effectiveness of the agent framework for video diffusion acceleration.

items.title: Researchers propose MEDIC, a dualistic meta-learning strategy to improve open set domain generalization by balancing inter-domain and inter-class boundaries, outperforming prior methods in experiments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Exploring Dualistic Meta-Learning to Enhance Domain Generalization in Open Set Scenarios
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced MEDIC, a novel dualistic meta-learning strategy designed to improve open set domain generalization by balancing decision boundaries across both domain and class distinctions. This approach addresses the challenge of label mismatches between source and target domains, which traditional methods often overlook, by simultaneously optimizing inter-domain and inter-class task splits to better detect unseen classes in new domains.

MEDIC overcomes the limitations of previous one-vs-all classifiers that tend to over-reject out-of-distribution data due to imbalanced positive and negative samples. Experimental results demonstrate that MEDIC not only surpasses existing methods in open set scenarios but also maintains strong performance in conventional closed set generalization tasks, highlighting its effectiveness and versatility in domain generalization challenges.
items.description:

This approach addresses the challenge of label mismatches between source and target domains, which traditional methods often overlook, by simultaneously optimizing inter-domain and inter-class task splits to better detect unseen classes in new domains.

MEDIC overcomes the limitations of previous one-vs-all classifiers that tend to over-reject out-of-distribution data due to imbalanced positive and negative samples. Experimental results demonstrate that MEDIC not only surpasses existing methods in open set scenarios but also maintains strong performance in conventional closed set generalization tasks, highlighting its effectiveness and versatility in domain generalization challenges.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.23758v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Domain generalization learns from multiple source domains to generalize to unseen target domains. However, it often neglects the realistic case of label mismatch between source and target. Open set domain generalization is then proposed to recognize unseen classes in unseen domains. A simple approach trains one-vs-all classifiers to separate each class and detect outliers as unknown. Yet, the imbalance between few positive samples and many negative samples skews the decision boundary towards the positive ones, leading the model to over-reject out-of-distribution data, even from known classes in unseen domains. In this paper, we propose a novel meta-learning stategy called dualistic MEta-learning with joint DomaIn-Class matching (MEDIC), which considers implicit gradient matching towards inter-domain and inter-class task splits simultaneously to find optimal boundaries balanced for both domains and classes. Experimental results show that MEDIC not only outperforms prior methods in open set scenarios, but also maintains competitive close set generalization ability.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate reinforcement learning for real-time trigger threshold tuning at the Large Hadron Collider, improving signal efficiency and background rate control on real collision data [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning to Trigger: Reinforcement Learning at the Large Hadron Collider
items.summary:
Researchers have applied reinforcement learning to optimize real-time event filtering thresholds at the Large Hadron Collider, enhancing signal detection efficiency while maintaining control over background noise. By treating threshold tuning as a sequential decision-making problem, their approach dynamically adjusts trigger settings based on streaming data, improving performance compared to static, hand-tuned configurations.

The team adapted Group-Filtered Policy Optimization (GFPO) for this streaming control task and tested it on two types of triggers: one sensitive to pileup variations and another designed for anomaly detection. Their method increased the time intervals during which background rates stayed within target ranges by up to 56% on real collision data, also boosting signal efficiency without requiring fine-tuning. This work represents the first successful demonstration of reinforcement learning-based trigger control on actual Large Hadron Collider data, with code made publicly available for further research.

By treating threshold tuning as a sequential decision-making problem, their approach dynamically adjusts trigger settings based on streaming data, improving performance compared to static, hand-tuned configurations.

The team adapted Group-Filtered Policy Optimization (GFPO) for this streaming control task and tested it on two types of triggers: one sensitive to pileup variations and another designed for anomaly detection. Their method increased the time intervals during which background rates stayed within target ranges by up to 56% on real collision data, also boosting signal efficiency without requiring fine-tuning. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.23993v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: High-throughput scientific facilities such as the Large Hadron Collider depend on real-time event filtering (\textit{triggering}) under tight constraints on bandwidth, latency, and storage. In practice, trigger menus are largely static and hand-tuned and can become suboptimal as detector conditions, pileup, and background composition drift over time. We cast online threshold tuning as a sequential decision-making problem: a reinforcement learning agent ingests streaming summaries of recent rates and signal-sensitive features and updates trigger thresholds to maximize signal efficiency while tracking a target background rate within a tolerance band. We adapt Group-Filtered Policy Optimization (GFPO) to streaming control and introduce two variants (GFPO-F, GFPO-FR) that enforce background rate feasibility during training. On a benchmark that emulates realistic collider operation, we study two representative triggers: a total transverse energy ($H_{T}$) trigger sensitive to pileup variation, and an anomaly-detection (AD) trigger based on reconstruction loss for rare or non-standard signatures. On Monte Carlo streams, our agent increases the fraction of in-tolerance time intervals by 48\% ($H_T$) and 28\% (AD), with a cumulative gain of up to 2\% in signal efficiency on those in-tolerance intervals. This work represents the first successful demonstration of reinforcement learning-based trigger control on actual Large Hadron Collider data, with code made publicly available for further research.

items.title: Researchers propose FlowPipe, an LLM-enhanced conditional generative flow network framework for data preparation pipeline construction, improving accuracy by 11.96% and training speed by 12.5x on 74 datasets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: FlowPipe: LLM-Enhanced Conditional Generative Flow Networks for Data Preparation Pipeline Construction
items.summary:
Researchers have developed FlowPipe, a novel framework that enhances the construction of data preparation pipelines for machine learning by integrating large language model (LLM) capabilities with conditional generative flow networks. This approach addresses challenges in automating pipeline synthesis, such as complex operator sequences and inefficient exploration, by modeling the process as conditional probabilistic flow generation over a directed acyclic graph. FlowPipe incorporates deep semantic modulation using LLM-derived logical priors and failure awareness to improve policy decisions and avoid invalid states.

Tests on 74 real-world datasets across two benchmark suites demonstrate that FlowPipe outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving an average accuracy improvement of 11.96% and training convergence that is 12.5 times faster. The framework's source code has been made publicly available, supporting further research and application in automated data preparation for machine learning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.24679v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Data preparation pipelines improve data quality in machine learning by transforming raw tables into learning-ready data through sequential cleaning and feature transformation operators. However, automatically constructing such pipelines is computationally difficult because operator sequences are combinatorial and end-to-end evaluation is expensive. Existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) Multi-DQN methods still face three key limitations: decoupled value estimators weaken long-horizon credit assignment, dataset context is only weakly injected into the policy, and exploration is inefficient in a sparse search space with many invalid states. To address these issues, we propose FlowPipe, a unified framework that formulates pipeline synthesis as conditional probabilistic flow generation over a directed acyclic graph. FlowPipe uses Conditional Generative Flow Networks (C-GFlowNets) with a Trajectory Balance objective to connect terminal validation rewards with early pipeline decisions. It further introduces Deep Semantic Modulation through Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM), allowing LLM-derived logical priors to condition the policy's internal activations according to dataset semantics. In addition, FlowPipe incorporates failure awareness into the flow objective to avoid invalid states and concentrate search on high-potential regions. Experiments on two benchmark suites with 74 real-world datasets show that FlowPipe outperforms SOTA baselines, improving accuracy by 11.96% on average and achieving 12.5x faster training convergence. Source code is available at https://github.com/KunyuNi/FlowPipe.

items.title: Researchers find a consistent geometric gap between detection and control directions in language models, showing detection does not imply steerability across multiple models and scales [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Perfect Detection, Failed Control: The Geometry of Knowing vs. Steering in Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have identified a consistent geometric gap between the directions in language models that detect behaviors and those that control them, challenging the assumption that detection implies steerability. By measuring the angle between the detection and control directions across multiple models and scales, they found a significant misalignment, with cosine similarities far from the ideal value of 1 that would indicate direct control. This gap persists across different models and remains unchanged before and after instruction tuning, suggesting it originates during pretraining.

The study shows that while models can perfectly detect certain behaviors, such as hallucinations, the direction that triggers a refusal to produce such outputs is distinct and only partially aligned. Attempts to bridge this gap through rotation improve control but do not fully resolve it. Importantly, the researchers found that the geometric measure of alignment does not predict steerability, indicating that control depends on functional factors beyond static geometric relationships. This work highlights a fundamental dissociation between knowing a behavior and steering it within language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.24952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A central aspiration of mechanistic interpretability is controllability: if we know where a behavior is represented in a model's activations, we should be able to modify it. This rests on a hidden premise -- that the direction which detects a behavior and the direction which controls it are the same, or close. We test this geometrically: what is the angle between the direction that best detects a behavior and the one that best causes it? If detection implies control the cosine is near 1; otherwise it quantifies a detection-intervention gap. On Gemma 2-2B-it, output format (clean JSON vs markdown fencing) collapses both roles onto one axis. Hallucination does not: the model detects fake entities with perfect linear separability (AUC = 1.000 from layer 5), yet that direction sits at cos = 0.12 (about 83 degrees) from the direction producing a refusal -- a small, reproducible alignment, far from the cos = 1 that "detection is control" would require. A detector built from activations, with no chosen tokens, likewise fails to align (cos = -0.06). The gap generalizes: across four models from three families and two scales (1B-9B), cos stays in [0.12, 0.20], identical before and after instruction tuning (0.1197 vs 0.1200), placing its origin in pretraining. A 15-degree rotation toward the refusal direction partially bridges it -- 73% and 60% refusal on two held-out fake-entity categories at 1.8% false positives. We then ask whether this cosine predicts steerability, and it does not: detection is a high-dimensional class, not a single direction, and what separates the steerable case is functional, not readable from a static angle. The cosine is a weight-computable signature of the dissociation between knowing and steering, not a predictor of it.

items.title: Researchers introduce a 32,534-response double-marked GCSE dataset and find large language models agree with examiners as closely as examiners agree with each other across five subjects [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LLM Performance on a Real, Double-Marked GCSE Benchmark
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a dataset comprising 32,534 double-marked student responses from UK GCSE mock exams across five subjects, including handwritten work. They evaluated whether large language models (LLMs) agree with human examiners as closely as examiners agree with each other. The study found that top-performing LLMs often matched or exceeded the agreement levels between examiners, performing well on subjective tasks like English essays and complex handwritten math scripts.

The dataset spans 328 questions and reflects real exam conditions, providing a robust benchmark for automated grading. The models' agreement with examiners was consistent across subjects and did not heavily depend on model size, suggesting that cost-effective automated marking solutions are feasible. This research highlights the potential for LLMs to assist or augment human examiners in educational assessment.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.24973v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a dataset of 32,534 double-marked real student responses to GCSE mock exams (GCSEs are the UK's national exams, taken at age ~16), spanning 328 questions across five subjects and including handwritten work. We test whether off-the-shelf large language models agree with examiners as closely as the two examiners agree with each other. We find that models overwhelmingly agree well with the examiner consensus across subjects, with the top performing models agreeing more closely with examiners than examiners agree with each other. Models achieve high scores for subjective tasks like English essay marking, as well as handling complex and messy handwritten Maths paper scripts. Agreement is uniform near the examiner line, and not massively discriminated by model size, providing cost-effective automated marking solutions.

items.title: Researchers analyze entropy dynamics in intermediate layers of large language models to detect jailbreak attacks without additional training across multiple architectures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What Intermediate Layers Know: Detecting Jailbreaks from Entropy Dynamics
items.summary:
Researchers have identified that jailbreak attacks on aligned large language models (LLMs), which prompt policy-violating responses despite safety measures, can be detected by analyzing entropy dynamics within the models' intermediate layers. By examining token-level predictive entropy trajectories across layers using the logit lens, they found that changes in entropy over token positions provide a stronger signal of harmful intent than static entropy statistics. This signal is most pronounced in the mid-network layers rather than the final output layer.

The study tested multiple LLM architectures, including Llama, Qwen, and Gemma, and demonstrated that these entropy dynamics consistently distinguish jailbreak behavior without requiring additional training. These findings clarify how harmful intent is encoded internally and suggest that monitoring intermediate uncertainty patterns could improve defenses against jailbreak attacks in large language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25182v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Jailbreak attacks reveal a persistent weakness in aligned Large Language Models: carefully crafted prompts can elicit policy-violating responses despite safety training. While most defenses operate at the prompt or output level, it remains unclear how harmful intent is encoded within the model's internal representations. We investigate this question by analyzing token-level predictive entropy trajectories across layers of a frozen LLM using the logit lens. We find that static aggregate statistics of prompt-level entropy (e.g., mean, variance) carry little discriminative signal, whereas features capturing how entropy evolves across token positions, such as monotonic rank-based trend scores, are substantially more informative. Importantly, this signal is not uniform across model depth: it is concentrated in intermediate layers and degrades at the final layer, indicating that jailbreak-relevant structure is most pronounced in mid-network representations rather than at the output head. Across multiple models (Llama, Qwen, Gemma) and adversarial benchmarks, these entropy dynamics provide architecture-consistent separation without additional training. Together, our findings show that jailbreak behavior is reflected in structured intermediate uncertainty dynamics, clarifying both which entropy-derived features encode harmful intent and where in the network that signal is most pronounced.

items.title: Researchers present iLLaDA, an 8B masked diffusion language model with bidirectional attention, showing improved performance on general, math, and code benchmarks after training on 12T tokens and fine-tuning on 25B tokens [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Improved Large Language Diffusion Models
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced iLLaDA, an 8-billion-parameter masked diffusion language model that employs fully bidirectional attention and is trained from scratch. The model was pre-trained on 12 trillion tokens and fine-tuned on a 25 billion-token instruction dataset, maintaining the masked diffusion objective throughout. iLLaDA demonstrates significant improvements over previous models like LLaDA across general, mathematical, and coding benchmarks, showing competitive performance despite its non-autoregressive training approach.

iLLaDA incorporates variable-length generation for efficiency and uses confidence-based scoring for multiple-choice evaluations. Notably, iLLaDA-Base improved by 21.6 points on the BBH benchmark and 14.9 points on ARC-Challenge, while iLLaDA-Instruct showed gains of 14.5 points on MATH and 16.5 points on HumanEval. These results suggest that fully bidirectional diffusion training is a promising method for developing strong language models. The model weights and code are publicly available for further research and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25331v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern large language models are predominantly trained with autoregressive factorization and causal attention. We present \emph{iLLaDA}, an 8B masked diffusion language model trained from scratch with fully bidirectional attention. iLLaDA keeps the masked diffusion objective throughout pre-training and supervised fine-tuning (SFT), scaling pre-training to 12T tokens and fine-tuning on a 25B-token instruction corpus for 12 epochs. We further use variable-length generation for efficiency and introduce confidence-based scoring for multiple-choice evaluation. Compared with LLaDA, iLLaDA improves broadly across general, mathematical, and code benchmarks; for example, iLLaDA-Base improves by 21.6 points on BBH and 14.9 points on ARC-Challenge, while iLLaDA-Instruct improves by 14.5 points on MATH and 16.5 points on HumanEval. Despite its non-autoregressive training, iLLaDA also remains competitive with Qwen2.5 7B on several benchmarks. These results show that fully bidirectional diffusion training from scratch is a competitive path toward strong language models. Model weights and codes: https://github.com/ML-GSAI/LLaDA.

items.title: Researchers find that language models with lossy memory producing stale conclusions perform worse than models with empty memory, introducing reclaim evaluation to measure correctability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reclaim Evaluation: A Lossy Memory Is Worse Than an Empty One
items.summary:
Researchers have found that language models with lossy memory—where incorrect conclusions are retained but the supporting reasoning is lost—perform worse than models with no memory at all. This phenomenon, termed brittle memory, causes models to confidently produce stale or incorrect answers, whereas models with empty memory tend to abstain. The study introduces reclaim evaluation, a method that compresses interactions and tests whether corrections can recover the correct answers, highlighting that the ability to correct errors depends on preserving the original source information rather than the model's capability.

The researchers demonstrate that a source-first policy, which prioritizes keeping the recomputable source over derived conclusions, can restore correctability within the same memory budget when the source is compact and identifiable. This approach was validated across multiple models and real dialogue datasets, showing that errors in dropped sources can propagate and become uncorrectable over time, while the source-first method limits this effect. The study provides a controlled analysis with exact scoring and matched controls, and the authors have released the evaluation tools and conditions for further research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25449v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A language model's memory can be worse than having no memory at all. Give a model a memory that kept a wrong conclusion but dropped the work behind it, and it emits that stale value as a confident answer; give the same model an empty memory and it abstains. Across seven models this direction never reverses, a clean kill condition that none breaks. We call this brittle memory: behavioral, not the near-immediate information bound beneath it; only its magnitude is disposition- and task-dependent, not its direction. We measure it with reclaim evaluation: compress a drifted interaction at a fixed budget, then test whether a correction recovers the known answer, scored against ground truth with no judge. Correctability is bottlenecked by whether the answer-determining source survives, not by capability. A one-line source-first policy (keep the recomputable source, drop the re-derivable conclusion) restores correctability at equal budget where that source is compact and identifiable; a length-matched control rules out added text as the cause. The hand-built oracle reaches 1.00; a one-prompt deployable version reclaims 0.49-0.88. The stake compounds: chained through a memory loop, a single dropped-source error corrupts a growing span of downstream steps and stays uncorrectable, while source-first holds to a bounded budget horizon. The wall and fix replicate across three deployed memory systems and on real dialogue (MultiWOZ), and past the budget where the source no longer fits, the fix fails silently unless the note records completeness. This is a controlled study of a mechanism, not a benchmark: judge-free exact scoring, matched-budget controls, and validators built to come out false. We release the harness, conditions, and validators.

items.title: Researchers introduce BiPACE, a bisimulation-guided policy optimization method with action counterfactual estimation for LLM agents, improving validation success rates on ALFWorld and Qwen benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: BiPACE: Bisimulation-Guided Policy Optimization with Action Counterfactual Estimation for LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed BiPACE, a new bisimulation-guided policy optimization method that enhances the training of long-horizon large language model (LLM) agents by addressing limitations in existing stepwise group-based reinforcement learning approaches. BiPACE improves credit assignment by clustering steps based on behavioral similarity and applying action-conditioned peer baselines, eliminating the need for a learned critic or additional rollouts. This method significantly boosts validation success rates on benchmarks such as ALFWorld and Qwen, outperforming previous techniques like GiGPO and GRPO across multiple model scales.

BiPACE works by reducing the mismatch between state and action credit assignment through a novel clustering technique that uses the actor's hidden-state geometry as a proxy for bisimulation. Its Q-style estimator nonparametrically calculates local advantages, leading to more accurate policy updates. Experimental results show that BiPACE achieves higher success rates with only a modest increase in training time, demonstrating its efficiency and effectiveness in optimizing LLM agent policies.

The introduction of BiPACE marks a meaningful advancement in reinforcement learning for LLM agents, offering a practical and scalable solution to improve policy optimization without added complexity. The researchers have made the code publicly available, facilitating further exploration and adoption of this approach in the development of more capable and reliable AI agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25556v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stepwise group-based RL is an attractive way to train long-horizon LLM agents without a learned critic: it reuses multiple sampled rollouts to estimate local advantages. Its weakness is less visible but more fundamental: every group-relative estimator assumes that the steps it compares are equivalent for credit assignment. We show that current agentic variants violate this assumption through a state-action credit mismatch. The observation-hash partition is overly fine on the state side, creating singleton groups with zero step-level signal, while a single within-group mean is too coarse on the action side, mixing state-value estimation with action-specific credit. We introduce BiPACE (Bisimulation-Guided Policy Optimization with Action Counterfactual Estimation), a drop-in advantage estimator that fixes both sides without adding a critic, auxiliary loss, or extra rollouts. BiGPO clusters steps by cosine distance in the actor's own hidden-state geometry, an empirical policy-induced proxy for bisimulation that substantially lowers the singleton rate left by observation hashing. PACE then recenters returns within each behavioral cluster using action-conditioned peer baselines; its Q-style instance estimates a local Q(s,a)-V(s) nonparametrically. On ALFWorld/Qwen2.5-7B, BiPACE_Q raises overall validation success from GiGPO's 90.8 to $97.1\pm0.9$ over three seeds, and crosses the 95% threshold on every seed, which GiGPO never does within the same budget. On Qwen2.5-1.5B it reaches $93.5\pm1.2$ versus GiGPO's 86.7, and on WebShop and TextCraft it improves over GRPO and GiGPO at both model scales. The measured BiPACE-specific overhead is 11.3% of a single training-step wall time. Yet it changes the estimator's comparison unit from surface identity to approximate behavioral equivalence plus action-side counterfactuals. The code is available at https://github.com/TianxiangZhao/BiPACE.

items.title: Researchers introduce Weave of Formal Thought, a method combining rigorous syntactic validation and learned structural representations to improve code generation in large language models, reducing Python token cross-entropy by 14.3% [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Weave of Formal Thought
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Weave of Formal Thought (WoFT), a new approach that combines strict syntactic validation with learned structural representations to enhance code generation in large language models. This method introduces a formal engine and constrained decoder based on the full Tree-sitter specification, ensuring that generated code tokens always form valid program prefixes. Additionally, WoFT employs a latent-variable fine-tuning technique that integrates non-terminal grammar symbols into the generation process, allowing the model to retain important structural information adaptively.

By fine-tuning the StarCoder2-3B model on Python code using this approach, the researchers achieved a 14.3% reduction in per-token cross-entropy compared to a text-only baseline. This improvement demonstrates that incorporating discretionary latent syntax helps recover critical structural details that traditional flat autoregressive training methods tend to overlook, potentially leading to more accurate and syntactically valid code generation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25987v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) attain remarkable surface fluency on code, yet they neither formally guarantee the syntactic validity of their output nor leverage the hierarchical structure defining the target language. While existing constrained-decoding frameworks address the former, they operate under rigid assumptions that preclude critical lexical mechanisms -- including context-sensitive lexing, maximal-munch tokenization, and keyword extraction -- and only approximate vocabulary masking, sacrificing completeness. For the latter, code LLMs typically inject grammatical structure via predetermined policies rather than learning which structural information to expose. In this work, we introduce Weave of Formal Thought (WoFT), a paradigm uniting rigorous syntactic validation with learned structural representations. First, we present a formal engine and constrained decoder that is sound and complete with respect to the full Tree-sitter specification. By augmenting generalized LR (GLR) parsing with a speculative-lexing construction that maintains concurrent lexer-state hypotheses synchronized with a GLR graph-structured stack, our decoder admits every subword token extending to a valid program prefix and rejects all others. Second, we present a latent-variable fine-tuning method training the language model to interleave non-terminal grammar symbols directly into generation. Utilizing the reweighted wake-sleep (RWS) algorithm to optimize the importance-weighted evidence lower bound (IW-ELBO) of the surface text, the model learns to selectively retain formal derivations as an adaptive structural scratchpad. For Python, fine-tuning StarCoder2-3B with our RWS objective reduces per-token cross-entropy by 14.3% relative to a text-only SFT baseline, demonstrating that discretionary latent syntax recovers critical structural information that flat autoregressive training discards.

items.originalTitle: The Hitchhiker's Guide to Agentic AI: From Foundations to Systems
items.summary:
"The Hitchhiker's Guide to Agentic AI" is a detailed practitioner's reference that explores the development of autonomous AI systems from foundational large language model (LLM) architecture to full production deployment. The guide emphasizes the importance of understanding every layer of the AI pipeline, covering topics such as transformer architecture, training techniques, reinforcement learning from human feedback, and advanced reasoning models. It also addresses agentic AI concepts including memory systems, agent design patterns, inter-agent communication protocols, and multi-agent architectures.

The book combines theoretical foundations with practical implementation advice, featuring code examples and references to primary literature. It concludes with discussions on agent development frameworks, user interface design for agentic systems, evaluation methodologies, and strategies for deploying these systems in production environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.24937v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Hitchhiker's Guide to Agentic AI is a comprehensive practitioner's reference for building autonomous AI systems. The book covers the full stack from first principles to production deployment, organized around a central thesis: building great agentic systems requires understanding every layer of the pipeline, not just one. The book opens with the LLM substrate -- transformer architecture, GPU systems, training and fine-tuning (SFT,LoRA, MoE), model compression, and inference optimization -- treated as essential foundations rather than the primary focus. It then develops the alignment and reasoning layer: reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), PPO, DPO and its variants, GRPO, reward modeling, and RL for large reasoning models including chain-of-thought and test-time scaling. The second half is devoted to agentic AI proper. Topics include agentic training and trajectory-based RL, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG and Agentic RAG), memory systems (in-context, external, episodic, and semantic), agent harness design and context management, and a taxonomy of agent design patterns. Inter-agent coordination is covered in depth: the Model Context Protocol (MCP), agent skills and tool use, the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) communication protocol, and multi-agent architectures spanning centralized, decentralized, and hierarchical topologies. The book concludes with agent development frameworks, agentic UI design, evaluation methodology for agentic tasks, and production deployment. Each chapter pairs rigorous theoretical foundations with implementation guidance, code examples, and references to the primary literature.

items.title: Researchers analyze why accumulated orthogonal transformations improve length extrapolation in attention models but degrade at extreme context lengths, with experiments supporting theoretical predictions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Why Do Accumulated Transformations Extrapolate?
items.summary:
Researchers have investigated why accumulated orthogonal transformations, such as those used in PaTH Attention, improve length extrapolation in attention models but experience performance degradation at extreme context lengths. By studying a variant that replaces position-indexed angles with accumulated token-dependent rotations, they found a similar pattern of initial improvement followed by decline. Their theoretical analysis shows that accumulated orthogonal transformations become incoherent after many steps, suppressing attention to distant tokens and creating a finite mixing window independent of context length, which explains the observed behavior.

The study further demonstrates that while accumulated rotations enhance extrapolation beyond training lengths, they inevitably degrade without explicit control of far-token contributions. Experiments confirm these findings, showing that random and learned token-dependent rotations improve extrapolation compared to traditional methods, and that rotating values alongside queries and keys extends the effective range. However, models relying solely on rotations still degrade at very long contexts, whereas methods like ALiBi maintain stable performance, highlighting the importance of managing far-token influence in attention mechanisms.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.24975v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: PaTH Attention showed that replacing RoPE's position-indexed rotations with accumulated data-dependent Householder reflections yields strong length extrapolation, though performance degrades at extreme context lengths. We ask whether this depends on Householder-specific structure or reflects a general property of accumulated transformations along source-to-query paths. We study a simpler variant keeping RoPE's block-diagonal SO(2) rotations but replacing position-indexed angles with accumulated token-dependent ones. It shows the same pattern: improved extrapolation then degradation at long contexts. We prove the result extends to accumulated orthogonal transformations satisfying certain regularity conditions: their products become incoherent after finitely many steps, suppressing attention to distant tokens. Accumulated rotations of queries and keys create a finite mixing window independent of context length; per-token suppression learned in training transfers unchanged to any evaluation length, and high-dimensional concentration produces a score gap suppressing far tokens while near-route transport preserves the target signal. Conversely, a lower bound shows accumulated rotations must eventually degrade: as the far set grows, no rotations preserve the near signal without explicit far-mass control. For SO(2) rotations, rotating values too makes residual far contributions combine incoherently, extending the range. Controlled experiments support these predictions: random accumulated rotations substantially improve extrapolation over RoPE, learned token-dependent rotations maintain near-training-length perplexity far beyond the training context, and rotating values helps over queries and keys alone. Rotation-only models still degrade at extreme lengths, while ALiBi stays length-stable, consistent with the need for far-mass control.

Experiments confirm these findings, showing that random and learned token-dependent rotations improve extrapolation compared to traditional methods, and that rotating values alongside queries and keys extends the effective range. However, models relying solely on rotations still degrade at very long contexts, whereas methods like ALiBi maintain stable performance, highlighting the importance of managing far-token influence in attention mechanisms.

items.title: Researchers introduce Taxonomic Strategy Retrieval to reduce compounding errors in foundation-model agents during multi-step persuasion tasks, improving win rates and argumentative efficiency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Diagnosing and Mitigating Compounding Failures in Agentic Persuasion via Taxonomic Strategy Retrieval
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Taxonomic Strategy Retrieval (TS-RAG) to address compounding errors in foundation-model agents during multi-step persuasion tasks. These agents often face challenges where early mistakes affect long-term outcomes, especially in subjective environments like persuasion. TS-RAG introduces a categorical bottleneck that separates argumentative structure from content, reducing semantic leakage seen in standard retrieval methods and improving logical consistency.

Evaluations show that TS-RAG enhances the transfer of abstract logic across domains and enables less complex persuader agents to outperform stronger opponents, increasing win rates from 70.5% to 78.5% while boosting argumentative efficiency. The study also presents a Debate State Representation for detailed diagnostics, highlighting the importance of strict constraints to prevent evaluation failures caused by agent conformity.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.24976v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Foundation-model agents in multi-step, open-ended environments frequently suffer from compounding errors, where early mistakes contaminate long-horizon trajectories. While Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) succeeds in deterministic domains, agents in subjective tasks like persuasion experience severe problem drift and sycophantic conformity. We identify semantic leakage in standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) as a reproducible trigger for these failures, as standard RAG prioritizes vocabulary overlap over logical necessity. To eliminate this leakage, we introduce Taxonomic Strategy RAG (TS-RAG), a systems intervention that routes strategies through a discrete categorical bottleneck to decouple argumentative structure from topical content. Zero-shot, cross-domain evaluations demonstrate that TS-RAG significantly improves the transfer of abstract logic where standard semantic retrieval collapses. Crucially, TS-RAG acts as a "capability bridge" in asymmetric deployments, empowering lightweight persuaders to consistently defeat parametrically superior opponents (improving win rates from 70.5 to 78.5) and accelerating argumentative efficiency. Finally, we introduce trace-level diagnostics via a turn-by-turn Debate State Representation (DSR), demonstrating the necessity of strict constraints to prevent evaluation collapse via default agentic sycophancy.

items.title: Researchers find thinking tokens in reasoning models rarely change safety outcomes and often lead to over-refusal, challenging assumptions about deliberative safety behavior [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Do Thinking Tokens Help with Safety?
items.summary:
Researchers have examined the role of "thinking tokens" in advanced reasoning models, which are believed to enhance performance and safety by allowing models to deliberate before responding. Their study across several leading open-weight models found that the final decision to comply or refuse a request is largely determined early in the process, with little change during the subsequent thinking phase. This suggests that the apparent deliberation is more a form of prefix completion than genuine reconsideration.

The study also revealed that current safety interventions, designed to encourage deliberation, tend to increase over-refusal and suppress the limited deliberation signals present. These findings challenge the assumption that thinking tokens inherently improve safety and highlight the need for new methods that foster authentic safety deliberation in reasoning models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25013v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Today's reasoning models use thinking tokens to attain stronger performance on benchmarks than their instruction-tuned counterparts. It is also generally believed that this more "deliberative" mode should improve alignment and safety, by providing the model a safe space to consider whether its planned answer to a request violates its safety principles. We present evidence that this intuition is not always correct. Across frontier open-weight reasoning models spanning GPT-OSS, Qwen, Olmo, and Phi families, we find that the eventual refusal/compliance outcome is already strongly predictable via a trained head on the first token's hidden representation ($0.84$-$0.95$ AUROC and $\sim88\%$ balanced accuracy for predicting refusal/compliance) before any visible thinking. The thinking process turns out to be more akin to prefix completion than to deliberative revision, with the final outcome rarely changing after the first $\sim20\%$ of thinking, despite giving the appearance of deliberation at the text level ($\sim74\%$ of text-level deliberations occur when the response distribution is already locked to one refusal/compliance side). We also find that existing inference-time and training-based safety interventions, despite being motivated by the goal of inducing deliberation, largely shift model behavior toward over-refusal while suppressing already-scarce deliberation signals. Our results suggest that safety behavior in current reasoning models is much less deliberative than commonly assumed, and highlight the need for methods that induce real safety deliberation.

items.title: Researchers introduce LLM-ACES, a closed-loop framework using large language models for adaptive discovery of dynamical system equations, outperforming baselines on 122 ODE benchmarks with higher accuracy and sample efficiency [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LLM-ACES: Closed-Loop Discovery of Dynamical Systems with LLM-Guided Adaptive Search
items.summary:
Researchers have developed LLM-ACES, a closed-loop framework that uses large language models to adaptively discover governing equations of dynamical systems from data. Unlike traditional methods that rely on fixed datasets, LLM-ACES iteratively refines symbolic hypotheses and guides data acquisition based on disagreements among candidate equations, improving accuracy and efficiency in identifying ordinary differential equations (ODEs).

Tested on 122 ODE systems from ODEBench and ODEBase, LLM-ACES outperformed state-of-the-art baselines by achieving significantly lower median normalized mean square error and higher symbolic accuracy. The framework demonstrated robustness to noise and required only a fraction of the data compared to existing approaches, effectively recovering correct symbolic structures without introducing spurious terms.

This adaptive, feedback-driven approach addresses challenges in modeling complex dynamical systems with limited data, offering a more reliable and sample-efficient method for discovering underlying equations. Its success suggests potential for broader applications in scientific domains where accurate modeling of dynamical behavior is critical.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25039v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recovering governing Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) from data is a central challenge in modeling dynamical systems across scientific domains. Existing approaches cast discovery as a static inference problem over fixed datasets, assuming that the observed trajectories are sufficiently informative. However, dynamical systems evolve over large state spaces, and limited data can make multiple equations observationally indistinguishable, leading to identifiability gaps and the recovery of incorrect governing equations. To address this, we introduce LLM-ACES, or LLM-guided Active Closed-loop Equation Search, a closed-loop framework that jointly optimizes symbolic hypothesis construction and adaptive data acquisition. In LLM-ACES, a large language model (LLM) proposes operator priors that partition the large search space into distinct regions, within which candidate equations are fit to the observed data. The disagreement among these candidates guides the acquisition of informative trajectories, creating a feedback loop that iteratively refines both the hypothesis space and the discovered dynamics. On 122 ODE systems spanning ODEBench and ODEBase, LLM-ACES achieves the lowest median NMSE, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines by several orders of magnitude while achieving a high symbolic accuracy of 46.2% and 52.4%, respectively. Our analysis further shows that LLM-ACES is sample-efficient, achieving better performance with one-tenth the data. Furthermore, LLM-ACES's feedback-driven data acquisition makes it robust to noise and recovers the correct symbolic structure, while baselines introduce spurious terms that fit the data locally but obscure the true governing relationships.

items.title: Researchers present ASAP, an agent-system co-design using LLMs to integrate diverse hyperparameter optimizers and reduce wall-clock time in machine learning experiments [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ASAP: Agent-System Co-Design for Wall-Clock-Centered Auto HPO Research for ML Experiments
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced ASAP, a novel agent-system co-design that enhances hyperparameter optimization (HPO) in machine learning by integrating multiple hyperparameter optimizers using large language models (LLMs). ASAP addresses limitations of previous methods that relied on single-tool LLM replacements and iteration-based evaluations, which failed to handle diverse problems and did not reduce actual wall-clock time. By combining diverse optimizers and redesigning the optimization loop, ASAP improves efficiency and reduces total runtime without sacrificing performance.

ASAP leverages the reasoning capabilities of LLMs to select proposals from a pool of inductive-biased optimizers each round. Its system design includes a prefix-stable prompt to maximize cache reuse, speculation parallelism to hide latency during model evaluation, and a Self-Tuner that adapts execution parameters dynamically. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ASAP consistently outperforms existing baselines across various modern HPO tasks, highlighting the benefits of integrating multiple tools and co-designing agent and system components for practical machine learning optimization.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25207v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hyperparameter Optimization (HPO) is essential for maximizing machine learning model performance, and its core challenge is sample efficiency: finding strong configurations within a limited budget. Because every HPO tool relies on a surrogate prior that imparts its own inductive bias, individual tools struggle once problems become sufficiently diverse and drift from these priors. Motivated by the reasoning and generalization capabilities of LLMs, recent work has explored using LLMs for HPO and reports improved per-iteration performance. Yet these methods share two limitations with a common origin: they use the LLM as a single-tool replacement evaluated by iteration count. (i) Deployed in place of prior tools, the LLM is itself constrained by its pretraining objective to one family of inductive-biased proposals; this single-source setup still fails to handle the full diversity of problems. (ii) Per-iteration evaluation ignores that, in real runs, LLM inference or tool execution is paid serially on top of model evaluation every round, so iteration-count gains do not translate into end-to-end wall-clock gains. We present ASAP, an agent-system co-design that addresses both limitations. On the agent side, ASAP uses the LLM to integrate a diverse pool of inductive-biased optimizers and to select among their proposals each round. On the system side, ASAP re-architects the loop to reduce end-to-end wall-clock while preserving regret quality: a prefix-stable prompt maximizes KV-cache reuse across rounds; speculation parallelism hides the remaining LLM and tool latency under model evaluation via a relative-error accept test; and a Self-Tuner adapts the speculation threshold from execution logs off the critical path. Extensive experiments on diverse modern HPO tasks show that ASAP consistently outperforms baselines, underscoring the value of tool integration and agent-system co-design.

items.title: Researchers present Argus benchmark evaluating 35 uncertainty quantification methods across 4 vision-language models and GUI grounding datasets, revealing stability limits and calibration challenges [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Uncertainty Quantification for Computer-Use Agents: A Benchmark across Vision-Language Models and GUI Grounding Datasets
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Argus, a comprehensive benchmark evaluating 35 post-hoc uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods across four vision-language models (VLMs) and multiple GUI grounding datasets. This benchmark assesses the stability and calibration of UQ methods critical for computer-use agents that convert VLM predictions into executable GUI actions, highlighting challenges in maintaining reliable uncertainty estimates across different models and interfaces. The study reveals that while UQ rankings remain stable across datasets for a fixed model, they degrade significantly when applied across different model classes or observable interfaces, emphasizing the need for model-specific calibration.

Argus includes a 27-method open-weight matrix and an 8-method closed-source matrix, covering a range of techniques such as logit-based scores, sampling measures, hidden-state and density estimators, attention-based scores, and verbalized confidence prompting. The findings show that hidden-state and density-based methods offer the most stable performance among open-weight approaches, whereas certain methods like CoCoA-1MCA and verbalized self-assessment excel in specific scenarios. The benchmark also demonstrates that uncertainty rankings transfer well within models but poorly to closed-source vendors, suggesting that UQ methods should be recalibrated for each target system.

The research further indicates that score-level discrimination alone is insufficient for deployment, as conformal click regions shrink significantly when UQ is calibrated but suffer coverage loss under calibration-test or interface mismatches. To support further development, the authors have released detailed records, calibration and test splits, UQ scores, and analysis tools to facilitate regime-aware selection of uncertainty quantification methods in GUI agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25760v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computer-use agents turn vision-language model (VLM) predictions into executable GUI clicks, so reliable uncertainty estimates are essential for rejection, calibration, miss-severity ranking, and spatial safety regions. Yet evidence on post-hoc uncertainty quantification (UQ) for these agents is fragmented across isolated model and dataset pairs, leaving it unclear whether UQ rankings stay stable when the agent, benchmark, or observable interface changes. We present Argus, a cross-regime benchmark for post-hoc UQ in single-step executable GUI grounding: a 27-method open-weight matrix over 4 VLM agents and 4 datasets, plus an 8-method closed-source matrix across 3 frontier vendors where logits, hidden states, and attention maps are unavailable. Evaluated methods span logit-based scores, sampling and consistency measures, hidden-state and density estimators (Mahalanobis, SAPLMA), attention-based scores, P(True) and verbalised-confidence prompting, and split-conformal prediction. The main finding is selective transfer: UQ rankings are stable across datasets for a fixed model, but degrade across model classes and observable interfaces. Hidden-state and density methods are the most stable open-weight family, while CoCoA-1MCA, Focus, sampling-based scores, and verbalised self-assessment win in specific regimes. Within-model ranking transfer is strong (Spearman rho up to 0.969), but cross-tier transfer to closed-source vendors averages only +0.08, so closed-source UQ should be reranked on the target rather than extrapolated. Conformal click regions show score-level discrimination is not enough for deployment: locally weighted disks shrink radii by 40-60% when the plug-in UQ is calibrated, but coverage degrades under calibration-test or interface mismatch. outputCleanup.description:
Researchers have introduced Argus, a comprehensive benchmark evaluating 35 post-hoc uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods across four vision-language models (VLMs) and multiple GUI grounding datasets. This benchmark assesses the stability and calibration of UQ methods critical for computer-use agents that convert VLM predictions into executable GUI actions, highlighting challenges in maintaining reliable uncertainty estimates across different models and interfaces. The study reveals that while UQ rankings remain stable across datasets for a fixed model, they degrade significantly when applied across different model classes or observable interfaces, emphasizing the need for model-specific calibration.

Argus includes a 27-method open-weight matrix and an 8-method closed-source matrix, covering a range of techniques such as logit-based scores, sampling measures, hidden-state and density estimators, attention-based scores, and verbalized confidence prompting. The findings show that hidden-state and density-based methods offer the most stable performance among open-weight approaches, whereas certain methods like CoCoA-1MCA and verbalized self-assessment excel in specific scenarios. The benchmark also demonstrates that uncertainty rankings transfer well within models but poorly to closed-source vendors, suggesting that UQ methods should be recalibrated for each target system.

The research further indicates that score-level discrimination alone is insufficient for deployment, as conformal click regions shrink significantly when UQ is calibrated but suffer coverage loss under calibration-test or interface mismatches. To support further development, the authors have released detailed records, calibration and test splits, UQ scores, and analysis tools to facilitate regime-aware selection of uncertainty quantification methods in GUI agents.

items.title: Researchers present a space-efficient streaming algorithm for language generation with polynomial memory bounds and characterize memory requirements for exact identification in DFA-recognized languages
items.originalTitle: Space-Efficient Language Generation in the Limit
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a space-efficient streaming algorithm for language generation that operates within polynomial memory bounds. The algorithm focuses on languages recognized by deterministic finite automata (DFAs) with limited states and alphabet size, aiming to produce a hypothesis language that closely approximates the target language while minimizing omitted strings. They demonstrate that exact identification of the target language requires exponential space, but their polynomial-space algorithm achieves a bounded generation gap and captures all sufficiently long strings in the target language.

The study establishes a clear boundary between polynomial-space approximate generation and exponential-space exact identification by providing both an upper bound algorithm and a near-matching lower bound derived from communication complexity. This work advances the understanding of memory requirements for language learning in streaming settings and highlights the trade-offs between memory usage and accuracy in language generation tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25777v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We initiate a resource-aware theory of \textit{language generation in the limit} under the minimal constraint of space efficiency. In our framework, a learner observes an adversarial positive stream from a target language $K$ and must eventually output a hallucination-free hypothesis language $L \subseteq K$ while omitting at most $\Delta$ strings of $K$. We focus on $\mathcal{C}_{s,k}$, the collection of languages recognized by DFAs with at most $s$ states over an alphabet of size $k$, as the natural hypothesis class for memory-bounded learners. In the exponential-space regime, we prove that a learner can exactly identify the target $K$. Under a stricter memory budget, we characterize the strongest possible generation guarantees. In particular, we present a streaming algorithm using $\mathrm{poly}(s,k)$ space that converges to a hypothesis with generation gap $\Delta = O(k^{2s-2})$. Moreover, the learned hypothesis captures every string in $K$ of length at least $2s-1$. We complement this result with a near-matching lower bound through a reduction from a standard communication complexity problem. Specifically, achieving generation gap $\Delta \le k^{(1-\varepsilon)s}$ requires $k^{\Omega(\varepsilon s)}$ memory. Together, these results reveal a sharp transition between polynomial-space generation and exponential-space exact identification.

items.title: Researchers introduce Autodata, an AI agent trained to act as a data scientist creating high quality synthetic training and evaluation data with improved performance across multiple reasoning tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Autodata: An agentic data scientist to create high quality synthetic data
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Autodata, an AI agent designed to function as a data scientist by generating high-quality synthetic training and evaluation data. This method involves training the agent through meta-optimization to enhance its ability to produce stronger datasets, leading to improved performance across various reasoning tasks including computer science research, legal reasoning, and mathematical problem-solving.

The team implemented a practical approach called Agentic Self-Instruct and demonstrated that meta-optimizing the data scientist agent itself results in even greater performance gains compared to traditional synthetic data creation methods. This agentic data creation approach offers a novel way to leverage increased computational resources for producing higher quality training data, potentially transforming the process of building AI datasets.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25996v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Autodata, a general method that enables AI agents to act as data scientists who build high quality training and evaluation data. We show how to train (meta-optimize) such a data scientist agent, so that it learns to create even stronger data. We describe the overall formulation, and a specific practical implementation, Agentic Self-Instruct. We conduct experiments on computer science research tasks, legal reasoning tasks and reasoning with mathematical objects, where we obtain improved results compared to classical synthetic dataset creation methods. Further, meta-optimizing the data scientist agent itself delivers an even larger performance uplift. Agentic data creation provides a way to convert increased inference compute into higher quality model training. Overall, we believe this direction has the potential to change the way we build AI data.

items.title: Researchers find small language models can unlearn previously acquired rules during pretraining based on corpus support frequency, with asymmetric control over rule survival and no recovery after removal [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Natural Ungrokking: Asymmetric Control of Which Rules Survive Pretraining
items.summary:
Researchers have discovered that small language models can unlearn previously acquired linguistic rules during pretraining, a phenomenon they term "natural ungrokking." In experiments, a model initially learned to correctly associate pronouns with gendered names but later lost this ability despite continued exposure to supporting data. The survival of learned rules depends on how frequently the training corpus reinforces them, with competing patterns able to displace established rules without leaving traces in the loss curve.

The study found that the frequency of rule support in the training data predicts whether a rule persists, while the ratio of data to model parameters influences the extent of rule degradation. This dynamic was observed across multiple training runs and model scales, including public Pythia checkpoints. Notably, once a rule is lost, attempts to restore it by reintroducing strong supporting evidence fail, indicating an asymmetric control over rule retention. These findings highlight the complex interplay between training data and model behavior during pretraining and suggest limitations in the reversibility of learned knowledge.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26050v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Midway through an ordinary pretraining run, a small language model learns the pronoun-gender rule: cued with a girl's name ("Sue cried because"), it resolves the next pronoun to she, generalizing to held-out probes (0.94 by step 925). By step 3,500 the same model scores near zero on the same probes, although the rule's evidence is still in the training data. We call this within-run reversal natural ungrokking: the corpus decides, with no trace in the loss curve, which learned rules a model keeps. Which rules survive is predictable from one corpus statistic: how often the training stream shows the rule winning. Across un-intervened runs (two corpora, three budgets, three seeds), support frequency decides a rule's fate; the data-to-parameter ratio only modulates how deeply a doomed rule falls. The same emerge-then-collapse dynamics appear in public Pythia checkpoints, collapse depth ordered by model scale as predicted. The forgetting is a displacement: a competing surface pattern out-competes the rule, and the log-probability margin between them crosses zero within 100 training steps of the behavioral collapse. Control over this fate is asymmetric: the same edit that destroys a rule on demand cannot restore it. Flipping support to counter-evidence in place kills the rule with monotone dose-response in two unrelated rules; but injecting support back, even to 450 times the level that naturally sustains it, buys no recovery. Every confirmatory threshold and prediction was pre-registered before the data it governed was read.

items.title: Researchers analyze climate discourse differences between paid Meta ads and organic Bluesky posts from July 2024 to September 2025 using interpretable thematic discovery with large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Paid Voices vs. Public Feeds: Interpretable Cross-Platform Theme-Based Analysis of Climate Discourse
items.summary:
Researchers conducted a comparative analysis of climate discourse between paid advertisements on Meta and organic posts on Bluesky from July 2024 to September 2025. They developed an interpretable thematic discovery method using large language models to cluster and label text themes without predefined topics. The study found that paid ads focus on promoting specific climate solutions in a formal and forward-looking manner, while organic posts emphasize systemic critique with a crisis-oriented, scientific perspective.

The analysis highlights systematic differences in how climate change is discussed across these platforms, reflecting the distinct nature of institutionally produced messaging versus user-driven conversation. The researchers also demonstrated the practical value of their thematic approach through tasks like stance prediction and theme-guided retrieval. Although centered on climate communication, the framework can be applied to analyze thematic differences across various communication environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2601.13317v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Climate discourse online shapes public understanding of climate change and informs political and policy debate, yet it unfolds across structurally different environments: paid advertising platforms host targeted, institutionally produced messaging, while public social media reflects largely organic, user-driven discussion. We present a comparative analysis of climate discourse across paid advertisements on Meta (previously Facebook) and public posts on Bluesky from July 2024 to September 2025. To support it, we develop an interpretable thematic discovery pipeline that clusters texts by semantic similarity and uses large language models (LLMs) to label clusters with concise, human-interpretable themes, requiring no predefined topic inventory or seed set. Using these themes, we find the two environments diverge systematically: paid advertising centers on strategic promotion of specific solutions in a formal, forward-looking register, whereas organic discourse centers on systemic critique in a crisis-oriented, scientifically grounded one. We also evaluate the utility of the discovered themes through downstream stance prediction and theme-guided retrieval tasks. While our analysis focuses on climate communication, the framework generalizes to comparative thematic analysis across heterogeneous communication environments.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate zero-shot cross-lingual confidence estimation in multilingual large language models using a monolingually trained linear probe without target-language retraining [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Shared Doubt: Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Confidence Estimation for Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a method for zero-shot cross-lingual confidence estimation in multilingual large language models (LLMs) using a linear probe trained only on a single language. This probe predicts the correctness of answers in open-ended question answering tasks by analyzing intermediate model representations and generalizes effectively to diverse, unseen languages without requiring retraining on target languages. The study reveals that confidence-related features are concentrated in the middle layers of LLMs across different languages, indicating a shared confidence subspace.

The approach offers a strong baseline for confidence estimation that compares favorably with existing methods, especially since its zero-shot performance depends on the similarity between the source and target languages. This work addresses the common limitation of prior confidence estimation techniques that often degrade or need retraining when applied to multiple languages, highlighting the potential for more robust multilingual applications of LLMs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.31220v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Confidence estimation (CE), i.e., quantifying the reliability of a model's prediction, has attracted great interest in the context of large language models (LLMs). However, most studies focus on English, ignoring the multilingual reality of LLM usage, while many CE methods degrade or require retraining across languages. To address this gap, we investigate whether multilingual LLMs encode shared, language-transferable confidence features in open-ended question answering. We use a lightweight linear probe that predicts answer correctness directly from intermediate representations. Trained monolingually, the probe generalizes zero-shot to unseen, typologically diverse languages without target-language supervision. Learned layer weights and multiple ablations reveal that confidence features concentrate in middle layers across languages, suggesting a shared confidence subspace. While zero-shot cross-lingual performance depends on similarity to the source language, the probe provides a strong baseline without any retraining and compares favorably to other popular confidence estimation methods.

items.title: Researchers propose Streaming-dLLM, a training-free framework that accelerates diffusion large language models up to 68.2X by pruning suffix tokens and using dynamic decoding with early exit [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Streaming-dLLM: Accelerating Diffusion LLMs via Suffix Pruning and Dynamic Decoding
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Streaming-dLLM, a training-free framework designed to accelerate diffusion large language models (dLLMs) by up to 68.2 times. This approach addresses inefficiencies in the block-wise diffusion process by pruning redundant suffix tokens and employing a dynamic decoding strategy with an early exit mechanism, which skips unnecessary iterations for tokens that have already converged. Streaming-dLLM maintains generation quality while significantly speeding up inference.

The framework improves spatial efficiency through attenuation-guided suffix modeling, which approximates full context by removing less informative tokens. Temporally, it adapts the denoising schedule dynamically based on confidence levels, enhancing decoding speed without retraining the model. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of Streaming-dLLM in optimizing diffusion decoding processes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2601.17917v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) offer a compelling paradigm for natural language generation, leveraging parallel decoding and bidirectional attention to achieve superior global coherence compared to autoregressive models. While recent works have accelerated inference via KV cache reuse or heuristic decoding, they overlook the intrinsic inefficiencies within the block-wise diffusion process. Specifically, they suffer from spatial redundancy by modeling informative-sparse suffix regions uniformly and temporal inefficiency by applying fixed denoising schedules across all the decoding process. To address this, we propose Streaming-dLLM, a training-free framework that streamlines inference across both spatial and temporal dimensions. Spatially, we introduce attenuation guided suffix modeling to approximate the full context by pruning redundant mask tokens. Temporally, we employ a dynamic confidence aware strategy with an early exit mechanism, allowing the model to skip unnecessary iterations for converged tokens. Extensive experiments show that Streaming-dLLM achieves up to 68.2X speedup while maintaining generation quality, highlighting its effectiveness in diffusion decoding. The code is available at https://github.com/xiaoshideta/Streaming-dLLM.

Streaming-dLLM maintains generation quality while significantly speeding up inference.

The framework improves spatial efficiency through attenuation-guided suffix modeling, which approximates full context by removing less informative tokens. Temporally, it adapts the denoising schedule dynamically based on confidence levels, enhancing decoding speed without retraining the model. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of Streaming-dLLM in optimizing diffusion decoding processes.
