items.title: Researchers propose Memini, an associative memory model with multi-timescale dynamics for continual knowledge updating in large language models, inspired by biological synaptic consolidation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Continual Knowledge Updating in LLM Systems: Learning Through Multi-Timescale Memory Dynamics
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed Memini, an associative memory model designed to enable continual knowledge updating in large language models (LLMs). Inspired by biological synaptic consolidation, Memini organizes knowledge as a directed graph with edges that carry two coupled internal variables operating on different timescales. This design aims to replicate biological memory dynamics, allowing new associations to be immediately usable, reinforcing repeated information, and enabling selective forgetting through a unified mechanism.

Memini applies the Benna-Fusi model of synaptic consolidation to external memory, reframing it as a learning substrate that adapts through its own internal dynamics rather than explicit management. This approach is intended to address the challenge that LLMs, typically trained once, face when deployed in constantly changing environments. The article presents an early-stage conceptual design and does not include experimental evaluation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.05097v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLMs are trained once, then deployed into a world that never stops changing. External memory compensates for this, but most systems manage it explicitly rather than letting it adapt on its own. Biological memory works differently: coupled multi-timescale dynamics make new associations immediately usable, strengthen what repetition confirms, and let the rest fade. We argue that external memory should follow a similar principle. In Memini, this view takes the form of an associative memory that organizes knowledge as a directed graph. Each edge carries two coupled internal variables, one fast and one slow, following the Benna-Fusi model of synaptic consolidation. From this coupling, episodic sensitivity, gradual consolidation, and selective forgetting are expected to emerge as facets of a single mechanism, reframing external memory as a learning substrate that reorganizes through its own dynamics. This workshop article describes an early-stage conceptual design without experimental evaluation.

items.title: daVinci-kernel introduces a reinforcement learning framework with co-evolving skill selection, summarization, and utilization for GPU kernel optimization, outperforming prior RL models on KernelBench [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: daVinci-kernel: Co-Evolving Skill Selection, Summarization, and Utilization via RL for GPU Kernel Optimization
items.summary:
daVinci-kernel is a reinforcement learning framework designed to optimize GPU kernel performance by dynamically evolving a library of reusable skills. It integrates three agents—a Skill Selection Agent that identifies relevant techniques, a Policy Agent that generates CUDA/Triton kernels based on selected skills, and a Skill Summary Agent that distills successful strategies—sharing a single large language model backbone. This approach ensures that only skills verified to improve execution speed are added, and the system is trained end-to-end using multi-turn reinforcement learning methods.
daVinci-kernel was evaluated on KernelBench, where its 14-billion parameter model achieved superior performance across multiple levels compared to previous reinforcement learning models, notably outperforming the prior leading model, Dr. Kernel-14B. The framework's combination of skill discovery, selection, and summarization represents a significant advancement in automated GPU kernel optimization.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.16497v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: GPU kernel optimization represents a paradigm where functional correctness is assumed and execution efficiency is the objective. We present daVinci-kernel, a reinforcement learning framework that couples skill discovery with skill exploitation through a dynamically evolving skill library. daVinci-kernel jointly trains three agents sharing one LLM backbone: a Skill Selection Agent that retrieves relevant techniques via BM25 and LLM reranking, a Policy Agent that generates multi-turn CUDA/Triton kernels conditioned on selected skills, and a Skill Summary Agent that distills successful rollouts into reusable skills. Candidate skills are added only after execution-based verification confirms reproducible speedups. All three agents share a single LLM backbone, are initialized via a structured SFT cold start on diversity-filtered data, and are then jointly optimized end-to-end with multi-turn REINFORCE and per-agent advantage estimation. On KernelBench, daVinci-kernel-14B achieves 37.2%, 70.6%, and 32.2% on Level 1, Level 2, and Level 3 under the Fast$_1$ threshold, outperforming the strongest prior RL-trained model, Dr\. Kernel-14B.

items.title: Researchers identify Memory Contagion, showing evaluator bias propagates across time in LLM agent memories even with perfect consolidation, with bias type and model generation affecting susceptibility [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Memory Contagion: Cross-Temporal Propagation of Evaluator Bias via Agent Memory
items.summary:
Researchers have identified a phenomenon called Memory Contagion, where evaluator bias propagates across time through the memory systems of Large Language Model (LLM) agents. Their study shows that when agents are influenced by biased evaluators, these biases become embedded in their experiences and persist in memory, affecting future agents even with perfect memory consolidation. The research highlights that susceptibility to this bias depends on the type of bias and the generation of the model, with length preference bias spreading in older models but not in newer ones, while authority bias does not propagate through memory in the tested scenarios.

The study involved experiments across different bias types and model versions, revealing that length bias can propagate at contamination rates as low as 20%, and that consolidation processes can either reduce or amplify bias depending on its nature. These findings expose a significant vulnerability in current agent memory designs and provide formal methods to measure how bias can persist and spread over time within LLM agent memories.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.23195v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on memory systems to maintain long-term coherence. Recent work shows that agent memories degrade during continuous consolidation. However, existing research assumes memories are derived from unbiased experiences. In this work, we identify and formalize a novel phenomenon: Memory Contagion -- the cross-temporal propagation of evaluator bias through agent memory. We show that when agents are trained or guided by biased evaluators, their experiences become biased; when these trajectories are stored and consolidated into memory, the bias propagates to future agents retrieving from the same memory store, even when consolidation is perfect (oracle). Across two bias types (length preference, authority bias) and four experimental phases, we demonstrate: (1) Memory Contagion occurs for length bias even with perfect consolidation on older models (Gamma_A = 13.18, DeepSeek V4-Chat), while newer models (V4-Pro, Claude) are immune, proving both that biased input is a sufficient cause and that contagion is model-generation-dependent; (2) authority bias fails to propagate in all 15 controlled multi-seed experiments (Gamma_A = 0.00), revealing that not all evaluator biases can cross temporal boundaries through current memory architectures; (3) No observed safe threshold: length bias propagation is detected at contamination rates as low as p=0.2. Our findings expose a critical but contingent vulnerability in current agent memory designs and provide formal tools for measuring cross-temporal bias propagation.

items.title: Researchers propose NaviGen to convert user interaction history into executable instructions for personalized multimodal content generation, improving image and video synthesis across multiple domains [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Navigating User Behavior toward Personalized Multimodal Generation
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced NaviGen, a novel approach that converts a user's interaction history into executable instructions to enhance personalized multimodal content generation, including images and videos. This method addresses challenges in encoding user behavior into a form understandable by language models and developing instruction-writing capabilities absent in existing data. NaviGen uses a dual identifier system combining collaborative and textual codes, enabling a two-stage training process that refines preference reasoning and aligns content generation with user intent through hierarchical rewards.

Tests across various domains such as products, games, and short videos demonstrate that NaviGen improves the specificity, relevance, and visual quality of generated content while also enhancing next-item prediction. The approach bridges the gap between user behavior and content synthesis, offering a more tailored and effective generation experience. The researchers have made their code publicly available to support further development in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.24196v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern AIGC pipelines deliver high-fidelity images and videos but presuppose a well-formed creation instruction, while end users rarely articulate visual details, leaving generators misaligned with user demand. We study personalized content generation, which turns a user's interaction history into an executable instruction for downstream synthesis, and identify two obstacles: behavior must be encoded in a form legible to language reasoning, and the model must acquire instruction-writing skill absent from both pretraining and behavior data. We propose NaviGen, which represents each item with a dual identifier coupling a collaborative code and a textual code as a behavioral substrate and a semantic bridge in one token stream. On this representation, a two-stage SFT+RL pipeline first distills preference reasoning and instruction writing from evolutionarily searched supervision, then aligns generation with user intent through hierarchical and self-consistent rewards. Experiments across product, game, and short-video domains show that NaviGen improves personalized image and video generation, strengthens next-item prediction, and yields more specific, relevant, and visually generatable instructions. Our code is released at: https://github.com/iLearn-Lab/NaviGen.

items.title: Researchers introduce DigenRL, a disaggregated reinforcement learning framework for diffusion-based generative large language models, achieving 1.56-2.10x throughput improvements over existing systems on 16-32 GPU testbeds [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Accelerating Disaggregated RL for Visual Generative LLMs with Diffusion-Based Parallelism and Trainer-Assisted Generation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed DigenRL, a disaggregated reinforcement learning framework designed for diffusion-based generative large language models (LLMs). This new system improves throughput by 1.56 to 2.10 times compared to existing diffusion RL systems like veRL-Omni and GenRL, by enabling flexible resource allocation, heterogeneous GPU support, and efficient task scheduling across 16 to 32 GPU testbeds.

DigenRL introduces innovations such as a generation-axis pipeline and time-step parallelism to enhance pipelining between rollout and training phases, an elastic trainer-assisted generation method that allows trainer GPUs to assist with rollout tasks dynamically, and a tightly constrained asynchronous strategy to optimize pipeline utilization. These advancements address limitations in current colocated execution models, which restrict resource scaling and deployment flexibility.

Extensive experiments using various generative models, including HunyuanVideo-13B and QwenImage-20B, demonstrate DigenRL's effectiveness in accelerating diffusion-based RL training. This framework represents a significant step toward more efficient and scalable reinforcement learning systems for visual generative LLMs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.24369v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a dominant post-training paradigm, driving the emergence of high-performance RL systems such as veRL for autoregressive large language models (LLMs). In parallel, diffusion-oriented RL algorithms, e.g., DanceGRPO and FlowGRPO, have rapidly expanded the scope of RL from language reasoning to diffusion-based visual and flow-based generation. However, efficient RL systems for diffusion generative LLMs remain underexplored. Existing implementations, e.g., veRL-Omni, still rely on colocated execution, which simplifies synchronization but couples rollout and training resources, limits heterogeneous deployment, and constrains independent scaling. To this end, we introduce DigenRL, a disaggregated RL framework for diffusion-based generative LLMs that supports flexible resource allocation, accommodates heterogeneous GPUs, and facilitates efficient task scheduling. To maximally reduce the execution bubbles in the disaggregated architecture, we propose: 1) a generation-axis pipeline (GAP) and time-step parallelism (TSP) in the diffusion architecture to enable finer-grained pipelining between rollout and training; 2) an elastic trainer-assisted generation (TAG) approach to enable the trainer GPU resources to dynamically assist in executing rollout generations; and 3) a tightly one-step constrained asynchronous strategy to further utilize the tail bubble in the pipeline. Extensive experiments are conducted on three hardware testbeds with 16-32 GPUs using HunyuanVideo-13B, Wan2.1-14B, FLUX.1-12B, and QwenImage-20B generative models. Experimental results show that DigenRL achieves 1.56-2.10x throughput improvements over state-of-the-art diffusion RL systems, veRL-Omni and GenRL.

items.title: BluTrain releases C++/CUDA AI training framework with native layers, outperforming PyTorch in throughput and memory efficiency on 124M-parameter GPT-2 model [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: BluTrain: A C++/CUDA Framework for AI Systems
items.summary:
BluTrain is a new AI training framework developed in C++ and CUDA that offers precise control over hardware execution while simplifying system complexity. Designed from the ground up, it features native implementations of all layers, including a typed tensor module with reverse-mode autograd, a linear algebra library, and a multi-mode distributed execution module. In tests training a 124M-parameter GPT-2 model on an 8-GPU system, BluTrain demonstrated superior performance compared to PyTorch, achieving higher throughput and up to 22% better memory efficiency without compromising numerical accuracy or model convergence.

The framework's architecture allows for extensive native tuning at every layer, enabling further performance improvements. By focusing on system-level optimization rather than just model architecture, BluTrain aims to set a new standard for efficient and scalable deep learning training.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.24780v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Progress in deep learning is, at scale, more a matter of systems engineering than of modelling: the behaviour of a model in training (its throughput, its memory footprint, and the numerical fidelity of the result) is determined less by the architecture itself than by how that architecture is expressed on the hardware. To achieve absolute control over this hardware expression while abstracting away systems complexity to make modelling seamless and eliminating the need for repetitive orchestration logic, BluTrain was architected from first principles as a robust, lightweight, and architecture-general training framework in standard C++ and the core CUDA programming model. Every layer is implemented natively: a typed tensor module with reverse-mode autograd, a linear-algebra library, a caching allocator, a multi-mode distributed-execution module, and an MLIR-based deep-learning compiler. In formal evaluations training a 124M-parameter GPT-2 baseline in FP32 on an 8-GPU 6000 Ada system, BluTrain outperforms industry-standard baselines in both throughput (sustaining an average of 407K tokens/s versus PyTorch's 395K tokens/s) and memory efficiency (achieving up to a 22% footprint reduction), while strictly preserving numerical fidelity and converging to a marginally lower final validation loss. With every layer explicitly open to native tuning, the performance ceiling is the framework's own to raise.

items.title: Workshop report outlines challenges and solutions for engineering reliable autonomous systems, focusing on verification, real-world deployment, and safe software architectures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Engineering Reliable Autonomous Systems: Challenges and Solutions
items.summary:
A recent workshop report from the Lorentz Center Workshop "Engineering Reliable Autonomous Systems" (ERAS) highlights key challenges and solutions in developing dependable autonomous systems. The event, held in June 2024 and co-organized by the FMAS and AREA communities, brought together researchers, industry experts, and sector representatives to focus on verification and validation techniques, real-world system engineering, and safe software architectures. The report presents a comprehensive catalogue of challenges and proposes pathways to address them, emphasizing both existing academic methods not yet widely adopted in practice and areas requiring further research.

The workshop aimed to bridge gaps between academic research and industrial application by fostering collaboration and outlining a roadmap for future efforts. This initiative is intended to support ongoing advancements in autonomous system reliability, ensuring safer and more effective deployment across various sectors where these technologies are increasingly prevalent.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.23760v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Engineering reliable autonomous systems is an important and growing topic in computer science. As autonomous systems become more prevalent, easy-to-use techniques for building them reliably are increasingly important. This workshop report captures and expands on the discussions at the Lorentz Center Workshop "Engineering Reliable Autonomous Systems" (ERAS), held from 10 to 14 June 2024. The workshop was co-organised by the organisers of the Workshop on Formal Methods for Autonomous Systems (FMAS) and the Workshop on Agents and Robots for reliable Engineered Autonomy (AREA). It brought together members of the FMAS and AREA communities, industry practitioners, and representatives from sectors where autonomous systems pose distinctive engineering challenges. The workshop focused on three main research topics: techniques for verification and validation of autonomous systems; engineering real-world autonomous systems; and software architectures for safe autonomous systems. Its main outcome is a catalogue of challenges in these areas and, most importantly, a pathway to solutions. Some challenges can already be tackled by techniques that are well known in academia but have not yet become regularly used in practice. Other challenges remain unresolved and require further research. This roadmap is intended to support future research and industrial collaboration.

items.title: Researchers present AutoSpec, a framework using inductive logic programming to evolve interpretable safety rules for LLM agents, achieving up to 94% false positive reduction and high recall across code execution and embodied agent domains [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AutoSpec: Safety Rule Evolution for LLM Agents via Inductive Logic Programming
items.summary:
Researchers have developed AutoSpec, a framework that uses inductive logic programming to automatically refine safety rules for large language model (LLM) agents. By evolving expert-designed rules based on user annotations of safe and unsafe behaviors, AutoSpec significantly reduces false positives while maintaining high recall, achieving up to a 94% reduction in false positives and improving rule accuracy across code execution and embodied agent tasks. The approach iteratively identifies key predicates to adjust rules, producing interpretable and auditable safety guidelines that generalize well to new scenarios.

AutoSpec operates by analyzing execution traces to find false-positive and false-negative examples, then uses inductive logic programming to generate and verify candidate rule modifications. This process converges within a few iterations, outperforming heuristic methods by up to 4.8 times in F1 score. The resulting rules balance precision and recall effectively, addressing the limitations of brittle hand-crafted rules and opaque neural classifiers in safety-critical applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.24245v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly automate complex tasks by integrating language models with external tools and environments. However, their autonomy poses significant safety risks: agents may execute destructive commands, leak sensitive data, or violate domain constraints. Existing safety approaches face a fundamental tradeoff: hand-crafted rules are interpretable but brittle, with overly conservative rules blocking safe operations (high false positives) while permissive rules miss unsafe behaviors (high false negatives). Neural classifiers lack the interpretability required for safety-critical deployments. We present AutoSpec, a framework that automatically evolves deployed expert-designed safety rules from user safe/unsafe annotations through counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS) guided by inductive logic programming (ILP). Starting from the expert rules and a stream of annotated traces, AutoSpec iteratively evaluates rules, mines false-positive and false-negative counterexamples, uses ILP to learn which predicates discriminate them, generates candidate rule edits, and verifies candidates to select the best revision. The key insight is that ILP efficiently identifies predicates that appear frequently in false negatives but rarely in false positives (or vice versa), dramatically pruning the exponential search space of rule edits. This continues until convergence, producing interpretable rules that balance precision and recall. We evaluate AutoSpec on 291 execution traces spanning code execution and embodied agent domains. AutoSpec raises rule F1 to 0.98 and 0.93 across the two domains, achieving up to 94% false positive reduction while maintaining high recall, and converges within 4-5 iterations. The ILP-guided approach achieves up to 4.8x higher F1 than heuristic CEGIS. The learned rules are human-readable, auditable, and generalize to unseen scenarios.

items.title: Researchers propose DynamicPO, a framework to prevent preference optimization collapse in LLM-based recommendation systems by prioritizing boundary-critical negatives and adjusting optimization strength dynamically [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: DynamicPO: Dynamic Preference Optimization for Recommendation
items.summary:
Researchers have identified a phenomenon called preference optimization collapse in large language model-based recommendation systems, where increasing negative samples paradoxically degrades performance despite lower training loss. This occurs because easily distinguishable negatives overshadow boundary-critical negatives that define user preferences, weakening the model's decision boundary. To address this, they propose DynamicPO, a framework that dynamically selects informative negatives near decision boundaries and adjusts optimization strength based on boundary ambiguity.

DynamicPO integrates two adaptive mechanisms: Dynamic Boundary Negative Selection and Dual-Margin Dynamic beta Adjustment. Experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that DynamicPO effectively prevents optimization collapse and enhances recommendation accuracy with minimal computational cost. The framework is designed to be lightweight and easily integrated into existing multi-negative preference optimization methods, with code and datasets publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.00327v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In large language model (LLM)-based recommendation systems, direct preference optimization (DPO) effectively aligns recommendations with user preferences, requiring multi-negative objective functions to leverage abundant implicit-feedback negatives and sharpen preference boundaries. However, our empirical analyses reveal a counterintuitive phenomenon, preference optimization collapse, where increasing the number of negative samples can lead to performance degradation despite a continuously decreasing training loss. We further theoretically demonstrate that this collapse arises from gradient suppression, caused by the dominance of easily discriminable negatives over boundary-critical negatives that truly define user preference boundaries. As a result, boundary-relevant signals are under-optimized, weakening the model's decision boundary. Motivated by these observations, we propose DynamicPO (Dynamic Preference Optimization), a lightweight and plug-and-play framework comprising two adaptive mechanisms: Dynamic Boundary Negative Selection, which identifies and prioritizes informative negatives near the model's decision boundary, and Dual-Margin Dynamic beta Adjustment, which calibrates optimization strength per sample according to boundary ambiguity. Extensive experiments on three public datasets show that DynamicPO effectively prevents optimization collapse and improves recommendation accuracy on multi-negative preference optimization methods, with negligible computational overhead. Our code and datasets are available at https://github.com/xingyuHuxingyu/DynamicPO.

items.title: Researchers find that a small group of Wikipedia editors significantly influences large language models' handling of animal welfare topics through targeted content edits [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Small edits, large models: How Wikipedia advocacy shapes LLM values
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that a small group of Wikipedia editors, known as the Pro-Animal Wikipedians (PAW), can significantly influence how large language models (LLMs) address animal welfare topics by making targeted edits to Wikipedia articles. Their 125 edits across 115 pages were found to heavily impact LLM responses, with models attributing a majority of relevant content to these edits specifically for animal welfare queries.

Using advanced data attribution techniques on models like Llama 3.1 and Llama 3.2, the study showed that PAW edits consistently ranked as the most influential sources for animal welfare-related questions, while having little effect on unrelated queries. Fine-tuning models on PAW content further improved their performance on animal welfare texts, confirming that coordinated Wikipedia editing campaigns can measurably shape the values and outputs of language models on specific topics.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.24890v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can a small group of volunteers shape how AI systems discuss animal welfare, just by editing Wikipedia? We show that they can. Wikipedia appears in nearly every major language model training dataset and is weighted more heavily than web-crawled text. The Pro-Animal Wikipedians (PAW), a group of advocates who add sourced animal welfare content to relevant articles, have made 125 edits across 115 pages. Using gradient-based data attribution (Bergson; MAGIC), we traced how these edits influence language model behavior. TrackStar retrieval attribution on Llama 3.1 8B found that PAW-edited sections made up 68 percent of the highest-attributed documents for animal welfare queries (p < 0.0001) but only 52 percent for unrelated queries about the same companies (p = 0.53): the model links PAW content specifically to animal welfare topics, not to the entities in general. MAGIC counterfactual influence estimation on Llama-3.2-1B, run across five random training-order seeds, gave the same picture even more sharply: in every seed, the top-10 most influential documents on animal welfare queries were all PAW edits (10 of 10, 5 of 5 seeds), while on general queries the same top-10 sat at chance (4 to 6 of 10). Mean PAW influence exceeded mean control influence on animal welfare queries with p < 0.0001 in every seed, an effect 6 to 30 times larger than on general queries. Leave-subset-out validation gave Spearman rho = 1.00 for all 10 runs. When we fine-tuned separate models on PAW content versus control content, each model performed better specifically on the type of text it was trained on: the PAW-trained model cut perplexity on animal welfare text from 12.4 to 8.4, while the control-trained model cut perplexity on control text from 16.1 to 11.4. A small, coordinated Wikipedia editing campaign therefore measurably shapes how language models handle the topics those edits address.

items.summary: Researchers have developed an error-aware TF-IDF retrieval-augmented generation framework to improve automatic speech recognition (ASR) error correction, particularly for low-resource languages. This new approach addresses common issues such as hallucination of rare entities and domain-specific terms by integrating a symmetric text normalization module with an error-aware TF-IDF algorithm that prioritizes corrective documents based on historical errors. Tested on the Persian subset of the FLEURS dataset, the method increased the error-aware hit rate from 53.7% to 90.9% and reduced the word error rate from 23.06% to 18.83%, achieving these improvements with minimal inference latency.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.24915v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: End-to-end automatic speech recognition systems frequently hallucinate rare entities and domain-specific terms, especially in low-resource languages. While retrieval-augmented generation frameworks can mitigate these errors using large language models, current architectures face significant challenges. They either rely on standard sparse retrieval that ignores phonetic misrecognitions or utilize heavyweight cross-modal embeddings that introduce high latency. This letter proposes a highly efficient, purely lexical error-aware framework designed to explicitly resolve phonetic and loop hallucinations. Our approach integrates a symmetric text normalization module with a novel error-aware term frequency-inverse document frequency algorithm. By constructing a sparse diagonal penalty matrix based on historical errors, the retriever mathematically prioritizes corrective documents containing specific high-risk misrecognitions. Evaluated on the Persian subset of the FLEURS dataset, our method increased the error-aware hit rate from 53.7% to 90.9%. In end-to-end evaluations, the integrated framework reduced the final word error rate from 23.06% to 18.83%, achieving significant accuracy gains with near-zero inference latency.

items.title: Researchers propose Dustin, a sparse verification framework that speeds up long-context speculative decoding by over 9x with minimal accuracy loss on Qwen2.5-72B at 32k sequence length [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Dustin: Draft-Augmented Sparse Verification for Efficient Long-Context Generation with Speculative Decoding
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Dustin, a sparse verification framework that significantly accelerates long-context speculative decoding in large language models. By combining lookahead signals from a draft model with historical attention from the target model, Dustin efficiently identifies critical tokens for verification, reducing latency caused by Key-Value cache loading. Tested on the Qwen2.5-72B model with a 32k sequence length, Dustin achieved over a 9-fold speedup in end-to-end decoding with minimal loss in accuracy.

Dustin addresses limitations of existing compression methods, which either sacrifice accuracy or incur high computational costs during verification. It employs a sparse estimation technique that limits importance scoring to a small subset of attention heads, enabling a 27.85x speedup in self-attention operations. Evaluations on benchmarks like PG-19 and LongBench demonstrate Dustin's effectiveness in improving inference throughput for multi-batch long-context large language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.24957v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While speculative decoding improves inference throughput for multi-batch long-context Large Language Models (LLMs), its efficiency is often limited by a verification bottleneck where Key-Value (KV) cache loading dominates latency. Existing compression methods fail in this regime: static eviction incurs accuracy loss due to saliency shift, while dynamic selection introduces prohibitive computational overhead during the verification path. We propose Dustin, a sparse verification framework designed for long-context speculative decoding. Dustin integrates lookahead signals from the draft model with historical attention from the target model to identify critical tokens with high fidelity across multi-step verification windows. To reduce recomputation latency, this approach further employs a sparse estimation scheme that restricts importance scoring to a minimal subset of attention heads. Evaluations on PG-19 and LongBench with Qwen2.5-72B demonstrate that Dustin achieves a 27.85x speedup in self-attention and a 9.17x end-to-end decoding speedup at a 32k sequence length, all with negligible accuracy degradation.

items.title: Researchers propose test-time adaptation with semi-supervised learning to improve AI text detection under continual distribution shifts, outperforming commercial models on adversarial examples [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Hitting a Moving Target: Test-Time Adaptation for AI Text Detection under Continual Distribution Shift
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a test-time adaptation method using semi-supervised learning to improve AI text detection amid ongoing distribution shifts, such as adversarial humanization, new large language models, and changes in human writing styles. This approach leverages the homogeneity of unlabeled samples during inference to adapt without requiring labeled data, addressing limitations of current supervised detectors that struggle with these shifts. Their method significantly outperforms commercial models, detecting 90.5% of adversarial AI-generated text compared to 24.1% by a leading commercial detector.

The study highlights that existing AI text detectors fail under both adversarial and natural distribution changes, while the proposed test-time adaptation remains robust. The researchers have made their code publicly available, facilitating further development and evaluation of AI text detection techniques that can operate effectively in real-world, dynamic environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25152v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deployed approaches for AI text detection often rely on training-time access to labeled datasets of both human-written and AI-generated text. This approach is vulnerable to three types of distribution shifts that occur continually post-deployment, and for which labeled data is often unavailable: adversarial humanization, new LLMs being released, and temporal drift in human writing. Simultaneously, existing approaches do not leverage a key signal of LLM usage: inference-time homogeneity. We propose a test-time adaptation (TTA) approach, using semi-supervised learning, that adapts to distribution shifts by leveraging homogeneity among unlabeled samples observed at inference time. Empirically, we find that state-of-the-art supervised detectors systematically fail when they encounter distribution shifts in AI-generated and human writing, both adversarial and natural, while test-time adaptation with semi-supervised learning is largely robust; e.g., the commercial model Pangram detects just 24.1% of our adversarial AI-generated text, compared to 90.5% for our test-time approach. We establish that test-time adaptation is a promising framework for AI text detection in the wild. We publicly release our code (which includes code for model training, evaluation, and plots) at https://github.com/kkr36/llm_detection.

items.title: Researchers present a taxonomy of conversational memory roles and evaluate their impact on response quality and personalization in large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Memory Makes the Difference: Evaluating How Different Memory Roles Shape Conversational Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a detailed taxonomy of conversational memory roles and examined how these different types of memory affect the quality and personalization of responses in large language models (LLMs). Their study highlights that various memory functions, such as clarifying memory, can enhance factual accuracy and personalization, while irrelevant memory can reduce topic relevance and degrade response quality. This work introduces a user-centric evaluation framework that better captures the nuances of conversational responses compared to traditional reference-based methods.

Through experiments on long-term datasets and advanced LLMs, the researchers demonstrated that memory roles significantly influence how conversational agents respond under different contexts. Their findings suggest that leveraging specific memory types can improve the personalization and correctness of responses, offering new directions for enhancing conversational AI systems despite the capabilities of current frontier models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25361v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prior research on memory mechanism in RAG-based conversational system has emphasized how memory is stored and retrieved. However, far less is known about how memories with different functional roles influence response quality. Specifically, how they shape an agent's responses under varying conversational contexts and whether they lead to substantively different response behaviors. Existing evaluations in conversational system are also largely reference-based, insufficiently capturing the nuances in responses that may address users' preferences differently. In this work, we probe the impact of different memory types in shaping agents' responses. We present a fine-grained taxonomy of conversational memory, classify retrieved memories into different role types, and design a user-centric evaluation framework that simulates user perspectives. Through comparative experiments on long-term datasets and frontier LLMs, our analysis reveal many differentiated effects of memories: e.g., clarifying memory improves responses' factual accuracy and constraint awareness, making them more correct and personalized; irrelevant memory reduces topic relevance and degrades constraint awareness. Despite the power of frontier LLMs, these findings shed light on how different memory types can be leveraged to produce more personalized responses and inspire further research in this direction.

items.title: Researchers develop neural machine translation systems for low-resource Tangkhul-English language pair using ByT5-large and mT5-small models, achieving BLEU score of 39.97 on test set [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Neural Machine Translation for Low-Resource Tangkhul--English
items.summary:
Researchers have developed neural machine translation systems for the low-resource Tangkhul-English language pair, using ByT5-large and mT5-small models fine-tuned on a corpus of 38,336 parallel sentences. The primary ByT5-large system achieved a BLEU score of 39.97 on a test set of 3,856 sentences, demonstrating promising results for this under-resourced Tibeto-Burman language spoken in Manipur, India.

The study highlights challenges related to Tangkhul's Latin-script diacritics and the domain bias of the training data, which includes biblical texts, stories, and conversational material. The researchers suggest that future improvements could come from diversifying the data and adapting the models to different domains to enhance translation quality further.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25365v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a study on low-resource machine translation for the Tangkhul-English (nmf-en) language pair. Tangkhul is a severely under-resourced Tibeto-Burman language spoken primarily in Manipur, India, with virtually no prior natural language processing infrastructure. We describe two systems: (1) a primary system based on ByT5-large fine-tuned on 38,336 Tangkhul-English parallel sentence pairs, and (2) a contrastive system based on mT5-small fine-tuned on the same corpus. Our primary ByT5-large system achieves a corpus BLEU score of 39.97, chrF++ of 58.07, BERTScore F1 of 0.8104, and COMET (wmt22-comet-da) of 0.7302 on a held-out test set of 3,856 sentences. We further discuss the orthographic challenges specific to Tangkhul's Latin-script diacritics, the domain bias of our training corpus (which comprises biblical text, stories, and conversational data), and avenues for future improvement through data diversification and domain adaptation.

items.title: Researchers present a red teaming framework for large language models that uses multi-role models to expose unfaithfulness, increasing adversarial attack success by up to 7.9% in question-answering tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: A Red Teaming Framework for Large Language Models: A Case Study on Faithfulness Evaluation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a red teaming framework for large language models (LLMs) that uses a multi-role system involving target, attacker, and jury models to identify vulnerabilities in LLM outputs. This approach effectively generates adversarial prompts that expose unfaithfulness in responses, increasing attack success rates by up to 7.9% in question-answering tasks and revealing reliability weaknesses.

The framework adapts across various evaluation tasks, including English question-answering and Arabic summarization, allowing comprehensive comparisons of model vulnerabilities. It highlights how structural constraints and architectural design choices impact model safety more than parameter scaling. While the method excels at cross-model and cross-linguistic vulnerability detection, it faces challenges in fully automating adversarial prompt generation across languages and detecting subtle unfaithfulness that does not involve explicit factual errors.

Overall, this multi-role red teaming architecture offers actionable insights into current LLM weaknesses and provides a scalable methodology for ongoing safety evaluation as language models continue to evolve.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25476v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance across natural language processing tasks, yet their deployment in high-stakes applications raises critical concerns regarding reliability, safety, and trustworthiness. In this paper, we present a red teaming framework that systematically uncovers vulnerabilities in LLM outputs. Our approach employs a novel multi-role architecture comprising target, attacker, and jury models. The attackers generate increasingly effective adversarial prompts while the jury rigorously evaluates response accuracy and consistency across tasks. In a case study, our strategy proved particularly effective at exposing unfaithfulness in LLM responses. Exploitative adversarial prompts increased the attack success rate by up to 7.9% in question-answering tasks, revealing weaknesses in reliability. The approach identifies how structural constraints in summarization can shape vulnerability patterns, with format limitations yielding measurable gains in faithfulness, and shows that architectural design choices typically outweigh parameter scaling in determining model safety. The framework's key strength is its adaptability across evaluation tasks, from English question-answering to Arabic summarization, enabling comprehensive comparison of model vulnerabilities. While it excels at comparing cross-model and cross-linguistic vulnerabilities, it faces challenges in fully automating adversarial prompt generation across languages. Our experiments also reveal limitations in detecting subtle forms of unfaithfulness that do not manifest as explicit factual contradictions, particularly across linguistic contexts. Overall, this architecture provides both actionable insights into current LLM vulnerabilities and a scalable methodology for ongoing safety evaluation as models evolve.

items.title: Researchers evaluate calibration and adversarial robustness of automated ASR scoring judges for LLM jailbreaks using 596 human-labeled samples, finding significant reliability and attack resistance differences [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: How Reliable Is Your Jailbreak Judge? Calibration and Adversarial Robustness of Automated ASR Scoring
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated the reliability and robustness of automated judges used to score attack-success rates (ASR) in large language model (LLM) jailbreak studies. Using 596 human-labeled samples from the HarmBench dataset, they compared two types of judges—a dedicated safety classifier and general LLM-based judges—against human consensus and subjected them to adversarial attacks. The study found that the classifier tends to over-flag harmful content with high recall, while LLM judges maintain high precision but show inconsistent recall, leading to varying ASR results depending on the judge used.

The two judge types also differ significantly in their resistance to adversarial manipulation. LLM judges were highly susceptible to simple framing attacks that altered their decisions 57% to 100% of the time, whereas the dedicated classifier was more resistant to such surface attacks but vulnerable to a white-box gradient-based attack that flipped 70% of confident true positives. An audit confirmed that these attacks did not remove harmful content, indicating that many reported ASR figures relying on automated judges may be unreliable.

The researchers recommend that future studies report judge precision and recall based on human-labeled data, adjust ASR metrics accordingly, and include adversarial robustness checks for judges. Their code has been made publicly available to support transparency and further research in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25487v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Almost every paper on LLM jailbreaks and prompt injection reports an attack-success rate (ASR), and that number is assigned not by people but by an automated judge: either a safety classifier trained for the task, or a general chat model prompted to grade. The judge is rarely checked. We check it. Using 596 human-labeled completions from the HarmBench classifier validation set, we compare the two judge families against human majority votes and then attack them. The two families fail in opposite ways. The dedicated classifier over-flags (precision 0.835, recall 0.974); three different LLM-as-judges keep high precision (0.81 to 0.94) but show erratic recall (0.06 to 0.65), so the same responses produce very different ASR depending on which judge scores them. The two families also differ sharply in robustness. Wrappers that leave the harmful text untouched and only add benign framing flip every LLM-judge between 57% and 100% of the time, and a single prepended refusal sentence accounts for much of this (39% to 88%). The dedicated classifier resists these surface attacks (at most 6.7%), but a white-box GCG attack on its open weights flips 70% of confident true positives (21 of 30; 95% CI 54 to 86%) even at a small optimization budget. A two-annotator audit confirms the attacks leave the harm intact: every one of 80 sampled flips still contained the harmful content. Because a large and growing share of reported ASR comes from LLM-judges, many such numbers are unreliable both on average and under deliberate pressure. We recommend that papers report judge precision and recall on a human-labeled slice, report ASR corrected for judge precision, and include an adversarial check of the judge. Our code is released.

items.title: Researchers use MARBERT model to detect spam and analyze sentiment in 24,513 Arabic tweets to improve Saudi Telecom Company customer service [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Spam and Sentiment Detection in Arabic Tweets Using MARBERT Model
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a model using MARBERT, a variant of the BERT deep learning framework, to detect spam and analyze sentiment in 24,513 Arabic tweets related to Saudi Telecom Company (STC). The study aims to improve STC's customer service by accurately gauging customer sentiments expressed on Twitter, a preferred platform for STC users to provide feedback. The model was evaluated using precision, recall, and f1-score metrics and showed promising accuracy compared to existing methods.

The dataset included tweets categorized as positive, negative, neutral, sarcastic, and indeterminate, reflecting a wide range of customer opinions. This research addresses a gap in natural language processing for Arabic, as most sentiment analysis work has focused on English. By leveraging deep learning techniques tailored for Arabic, the study offers a valuable tool for enhancing customer satisfaction through better understanding of social media feedback.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25495v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Saudi Telecom Company (STC) is among the most popular companies in Saudi Arabia, with many customers. Yet, there is still a big room for improvement in users' satisfaction. Social media is the most robust platform to gauge users' satisfaction and determine their sentiments and critics. Twitter is among the most popular social media platform in this regard. STC customers prefer to use Twitter to write their feedback because it's a fast way to get responses due to the STC customer services account. One way to achieve customer demands and improve customer service is using the Sentiment Analysis tool. Sentiment Analysis on Twitter is highly used because of the significant number of tweets and the different opinions. Likewise, Deep learning is the best existing Sentiment Analysis method, and it has diverse models. Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) model is one of the deep learning models which have achieved excellent results in Sentiment Analysis for Natural Language Processing (NLP). NLP is mainly investigated in the English language. However, for Arabic, there is a significant gap to be filled. This study trained the proposed model using MARBERT and measured the performance using f1-score, precision, and recall metrics. We trained the model with an Arabic dataset of 24,513 tweets, including 1,437 positive, 13,828 negative, 5,694 neutral, 1,221 sarcasm, and 2,297 indeterminate tweets. The main goal is to analyze the tweets and get the sentiment to improve STC customer service. The proposed scheme is promising in terms of accuracy in contrast to existing techniques in the literature.

items.title: Researchers propose Semantic Frame-Level Multi-Task Self-Consistency to improve multi-intent spoken language understanding accuracy in zero-shot MAC-SLU benchmark tests [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SFL-MTSC: Leveraging Semantic Frame-Level Multi-Task Self-Consistency for Robust Multi-Intent Spoken Language Understanding
items.summary: Researchers have introduced Semantic Frame-Level Multi-Task Self-Consistency (SFL-MTSC), a new framework designed to enhance the accuracy of multi-intent spoken language understanding (SLU) using large language models. This approach addresses inconsistencies in intent-slot structures caused by decoding variability, especially in multi-intent scenarios, by decomposing predictions into intent-specific frames and applying domain-intent grouping and slot-level clustering to assess reliability before forming the final output. Zero-shot testing on the MAC-SLU benchmark demonstrated improvements in slot F1 scores and overall accuracy compared to traditional single-path inference, while maintaining stable intent accuracy across various settings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prompt-based spoken language understanding (SLU) with large language models (LLMs) often suffers from inconsistent intent--slot structures due to decoding stochasticity, particularly in multi-intent scenarios. In view of this, we propose Semantic Frame-Level Multi-Task Self-Consistency (SFL-MTSC), a novel structured aggregation framework operating at the semantic frame level. Instead of output-level majority voting, SFL-MTSC decomposes predictions into intent-specific frames, applies domain--intent grouping and slot-level clustering, and evaluates cluster reliability using path support scoring. Reliable frames are retained and re-integrated to form the final prediction. Zero-shot experiments on the MAC-SLU benchmark dataset show improved slot F1 and overall accuracy over single-path inference, while intent accuracy remains largely stable across most settings.

items.title: Researchers propose REVERIEMEM, a three-layer memory architecture for book-based role-playing agents that improves knowledge boundary fidelity by 34.6 points and achieves 79% win rate on narrative benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Staying In Character: Perspective-Bounded Memory For Book-Based Role-Playing Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced REVERIEMEM, a novel three-layer memory architecture designed for book-based role-playing agents that enhances the fidelity of knowledge boundaries by 34.6 percentage points and achieves a 79% win rate on narrative benchmarks. This system addresses common issues in long-narrative role-playing, such as characters using facts beyond their perspective and maintaining a monotonous style, by structuring memory into episodic, semantic, and personality layers that capture scene memories, visibility-tagged facts, and situation-dependent behaviors respectively.

To evaluate REVERIEMEM, the team developed KBF-QA, a benchmark consisting of 4,386 questions across eight novels to test knowledge boundaries. The architecture's performance on BOOKWORLD's narrative protocol demonstrates significant improvements in both maintaining perspective-bounded memory and generating character-grounded narratives, suggesting its potential to advance the realism and depth of AI-driven role-playing agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25632v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent LLM role-playing systems build character agents from novels by extracting characters, scenes, and relations. Yet long-narrative role-playing suffers from two failures: Factual Overreach, where shared retrieval or parametric memory lets a character use facts outside its perspective, and Stylistic Monotony, where profile descriptions flatten a character into a fixed voice. To address these failures, we propose REVERIEMEM, a three-layer memory architecture for book-based character agents. The episodic layer stores first-person scene memories; the semantic layer stores visibility-tagged facts; and the personality layer stores situation-dependent speech and behaviour patterns. For evaluation, we construct KBF-QA, a 4,386-question benchmark over eight novels for testing knowledge boundaries. REVERIEMEM improves Knowledge Boundary Fidelity by 34.6 percentage points over the strongest prior method. On BOOKWORLD's five-dimension pairwise narrative protocol, REVERIEMEM achieves a ~ 79% win rate, suggesting that perspective-bounded memory improves both boundary fidelity and character-grounded narrative generation.

items.title: Researchers introduce a framework comparing nine RAG scenarios including GraphRAG and Agentic RAG with context optimization, showing 19%-53% token usage reduction and identifying retrieval-generation gaps [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Is GraphRAG Needed? From Basic RAG to Graph-/Agentic Solutions with Context Optimization
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a comprehensive framework to evaluate and compare nine different Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) scenarios, including advanced variants like GraphRAG and Agentic RAG. Their study addresses practical use cases involving semi-structured knowledge bases and introduces a novel context engineering method that reduces token usage by 19% to 53%, improving efficiency in managing text and graph retrievals. The research also highlights a retrieval-generation gap, where increased retrieval does not always lead to proportional improvements in generation quality, suggesting that current retrieval-focused metrics may overestimate the benefits of advanced retrieval techniques.

The framework encompasses a range of scenarios from simple document-based retrieval to complex integrations involving hybrid text-graph retrieval, domain knowledge graphs, and multi-step agentic planning. By standardizing these scenarios and conducting extensive experiments, the study offers data-driven insights into when and how to deploy various RAG approaches effectively. This work aims to guide the development of production-ready intelligent RAG systems by clarifying the trade-offs and practical considerations involved in their implementation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25656v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As advanced RAG variants like GraphRAG and Agentic RAG emerge, one leading question is when and how to use them. Here, we introduce a framework for different RAG scenarios evaluation and comparison on semi-structured knowledge bases, including regular RAG, GraphRAG, Modular RAG and Agentic RAG. We provide implementation for 9 standardized RAG scenarios, and conduct experiments for a comprehensive comparison. These scenarios are designed for real use cases regarding data and domain restrictions, spanning from simple document-based retrieval to advanced features such as hybrid text-graph retrieval, integration with computed or pre-defined domain knowledge graphs, agentic multi-step planning, and agent-graph integration. Besides, we present a novel context engineering method for GraphRAG and Agentic RAG, addressing the context/memory overflow issues, efficiently managing text and graph retrievals with new representations and agentic loop design, leading to 19%-53% reduction on token usage. Moreover, further analysis identifies a retrieval-generation gap where expanded retrieval does not proportionally improve generation quality, suggesting retrieval-oriented metrics overstate advanced retrieval benefits. This work provides data-driven insights on when and how to use them for building production-ready intelligent RAG systems.

items.title: Researchers compare fine-tuned encoder classifiers and LLM-based judges for safety evaluation of large language model outputs across adversarial datasets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Do Encoders Suffice? A Systematic Comparison of Encoder and Decoder Safety Judges for LLM Adversarial Evaluation
items.summary:
Researchers have conducted a systematic comparison between fine-tuned encoder classifiers from the ModernBERT family and large language model (LLM)-based judges to evaluate the safety of LLM outputs in user interactions. Their study assesses whether encoder classifiers can effectively identify harmful content without significant performance loss compared to LLM judges, which are typically slower and more costly to deploy. The evaluation uses various adversarial datasets and benchmarks encoder classifiers against rule-based methods, fine-tuned LLM classifiers, and multiple LLM judge strategies.

The study fine-tunes encoder classifiers on judge-labeled data using a majority-voting approach and evaluates them on a gold-standard holdout set, measuring performance with metrics such as F1 score, false negative rate, and precision-recall. Results are analyzed by different attack techniques, including single-turn prompting and context manipulation, to determine where encoder classifiers align with or differ from LLM-based judges. The findings offer insights into when encoder classifiers can serve as efficient, cost-effective alternatives for safety evaluation in large language model applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25782v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs) in chatbots and everyday applications, companies increasingly need guardrails that are effective while remaining low-cost and low-latency. Safety evaluation of LLM outputs has generally relied on LLM-based judges, which can be effective but are often slow and expensive to deploy at scale. In this paper, we evaluate whether fine-tuned modern encoder classifiers from the ModernBERT family, including ModernBERT and Ettin, can reliably identify harmful LLM outputs in user-model conversations without substantial performance loss relative to LLM-based judges. We benchmark these encoder classifiers against rule-based prefix matching, fine-tuned LLM classifiers, and LLM judges using a range of judge-prompting strategies across open-source adversarial datasets. The LLM judges include evaluation methodologies from StrongReject, ShieldGemma, JailbreakBench, AILuminate, SorryBench, and a Claude-as-a-judge setup, as well as fine-tuned safety classifiers such as LlamaGuard 3 and LlamaGuard 4. The encoder classifiers are fine-tuned on judge-labeled data using a majority-voting label strategy and are then evaluated on a gold-standard holdout dataset to assess their performance relative to LLM judges. We report absolute performance using F1 score, false negative rate, and precision-recall metrics. We also break down results by attack technique, including single-turn prompting, decomposition, escalation, and context manipulation, to identify where encoder classifiers align with or diverge from LLM-based judges. Our findings provide guidance on when encoder classifiers can serve as cost- and latency-efficient alternatives to LLM-based safety evaluation.

items.title: Researchers propose SARA framework to align routing in sparse Mixture-of-Experts models, improving multilingual performance on low-resource languages across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SARA: Unlocking Multilingual Knowledge in Mixture-of-Experts via Semantically Anchored Routing Alignment
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced SARA (Semantically Anchored Routing Alignment), a new framework designed to improve the performance of sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models in multilingual settings, particularly for low-resource languages. SARA addresses the challenge where tokens from low-resource languages are routed to different experts than those for high-resource languages, limiting cross-lingual knowledge sharing. By aligning the routing distributions of low-resource languages with those of high-resource languages using a Jensen-Shannon divergence constraint, SARA enhances expert selection consistency across languages.

The team tested SARA on two large language models across five low-resource languages and three benchmarks, achieving performance gains over standard instruction tuning methods. For example, improvements of 0.8% and 1.2% were observed on the Qwen3-30B-A3B and Phi-3.5-MoE-instruct models, respectively, on the Global-MMLU benchmark. These results suggest that SARA effectively mitigates performance bottlenecks in low-resource languages and offers a scalable approach to boost multilingual capabilities in sparse MoE architectures.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25821v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures have emerged as an increasingly influential paradigm as they offer a strategic balance between parameter scalability and computational efficiency. However, low-resource languages, which suffer from a scarcity of high-quality training data, often have their tokens routed to different experts than those predominantly activated by high-resource inputs, which limits cross-lingual expert sharing. This cross-lingual routing divergence consequently hinders their efficacy in multilingual contexts. To address this issue, we propose SARA (Semantically Anchored Routing Alignment), a framework designed to transfer specialized capabilities from high-resource languages as anchors to low-resource languages. SARA explicitly aligns the routing distribution of multilingual inputs with high-resource semantic anchors using a symmetric Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence constraint. Unlike traditional distillation methods that operate on output logits, SARA directly aligns the internal routing distributions of MoE layers, encouraging mechanistic consistency in expert selection across languages. We conduct experiments on 2 LLMs across 5 low-resource languages and 3 benchmarks. Experiment results demonstrate that SARA outperforms standard instruction tuning, e.g., +0.8% on Qwen3-30B-A3B and +1.2% on Phi-3.5-MoE-instruct on Global-MMLU. Further analyses show that SARA effectively addresses performance bottlenecks in low-resource languages, providing a scalable pathway to enhance multilingual capabilities in sparse architectures.

items.title: Overview of HIPE-2026 evaluation on person-place relation extraction from noisy multilingual historical texts in French, German, and English with 17 teams and 40 runs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Overview of HIPE-2026: Person-Place Relation Extraction from Multilingual Historical Texts
items.summary:
HIPE-2026, the third edition of the HIPE evaluation series, focused on extracting temporally grounded person-place relations from noisy, multilingual historical texts in French, German, and English. The challenge involved determining whether a person was present at a location and when, using datasets from nineteenth and twentieth-century newspapers and early modern French literary texts. Seventeen teams participated, submitting over 40 runs that employed various methods ranging from large language models to lightweight classifiers.

The evaluation featured a three-fold framework assessing predictive accuracy, computational efficiency, and cross-domain generalization to address the practical needs of processing large-scale historical documents in cultural heritage contexts. Results highlighted the trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, and robustness in historical relation extraction, providing insights into current capabilities and challenges in this area. The paper presents detailed system descriptions, datasets, and findings, offering a comprehensive overview of temporally grounded relation extraction for historical documents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Was this person ever at that place, and if so, when? Answering such questions from noisy, multilingual historical documents is the central challenge of HIPE-2026, the third edition of the HIPE evaluation series. Moving from named entity recognition and linking (HIPE-2020, HIPE-2022) to reasoning about relationships between entities, HIPE-2026 targets two temporally grounded relation types: $at$, indicating that a person was present at a location at some point prior to a document's publication date, and $isAt$, indicating presence contemporaneous with that date. This paper presents the results of the evaluation campaign, which confronted 17 participating teams with the challenges of historical language variation, OCR noise, and indirect contextual cues across three languages: French, German, and English. The datasets include historical newspaper text from the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, as well as a surprise-domain generalization set drawn from early modern French literary texts. A distinctive feature of HIPE-2026 is its three-fold evaluation framework, which assesses predictive accuracy, computational efficiency, and cross-domain generalization, reflecting the practical demands of large-scale historical document processing in the cultural heritage domain. Across more than 40 submitted runs, results reveal a wide range of strategies, from state-of-the-art large language models to lightweight task-specific classifiers, and highlight the trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, and robustness inherent to historical relation extraction at corpus scale. System descriptions, datasets, and findings are presented and discussed, offering a detailed picture of the current state of temporally grounded relation extraction for historical documents.

items.title: Researchers introduce SpeechEQ, a benchmark and dataset for evaluating emotional intelligence in speech-language models across 2,265 dialogues and 15 EQ subscales [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SpeechEQ: Benchmarking Emotional Intelligence Quotient in Socially Aware Voice Conversational Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SpeechEQ, a new benchmark and dataset designed to evaluate the emotional intelligence of speech-language models in multi-turn dialogues. The framework includes 2,265 dialogues annotated across 15 emotional quotient subscales based on EQ-i 2.0 theory, along with a Spoken EQ (SEQ) score to assess sociolinguistic reasoning in conversational AI. This approach addresses limitations in current evaluations that focus only on isolated text or passive acoustic cues, overlooking the complex cross-modal reasoning needed for natural human-AI interaction.

Experiments using SpeechEQ reveal that existing speech emotion recognition systems and end-to-end speech-language models struggle to fully understand and apply paralinguistic cues. Although end-to-end models perform better than cascaded systems, challenges such as reliance on text shortcuts, alignment safety issues, and contextual memory gaps persist. These findings highlight significant barriers to developing truly emotionally aware AI systems. The SpeechEQ benchmark and a demonstration are publicly available for further research and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25990v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As multimodal conversational systems increasingly engage in spoken interaction, their ability to navigate paralinguistic social cues has become a critical bottleneck for natural human-AI communication. However, existing evaluations of machine emotional intelligence assess reasoning exclusively through isolated text or passive acoustic perception, overlooking the complex cross-modal reasoning required for active, multi-turn dialogue. We introduce \textsc{SpeechEQ}, a comprehensive framework designed to evaluate the sociolinguistic reasoning of Speech-Language Models (SLMs). The framework includes a validated dataset of 2,265 dialogues across 15 Emotional Quotient (EQ) subscales grounded in EQ-i 2.0 theory, along with a multi-turn evaluation protocol measured by our proposed Spoken EQ (SEQ) score inspired by human EQ assessments. Experiments show limitations in how both existing Speech Emotion Recognition and end-to-end Speech-Language Models understand and apply paralinguistic cues through speech. While end-to-end architectures outperform cascaded systems, \textsc{SpeechEQ} reveals that current multimodal models remain bottlenecked by a text-reliant ``modality shortcut,'' an alignment-induced ``safety trap,'' and ``contextual amnesia,'' highlighting the barriers to truly emotionally aware AI. Our benchmark can be accessed at https://huggingface.co/datasets/SpeechEQ/SpeechEQ and demo page at https://binomial14.github.io/speecheq-demo/

items.title: Researchers find multi-step tool-use reinforcement learning in large language models can collapse due to control token probability spikes and show supervisory signals improve stability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Why Multi-Step Tool-Use Reinforcement Learning Collapses and How Supervisory Signals Fix It
items.summary:
Researchers have identified that multi-step tool-use reinforcement learning (RL) in large language models (LLMs) can suffer from catastrophic collapse, where performance suddenly deteriorates due to unexpected probability spikes in specific control tokens. This disrupts the structured execution of tasks, although the models' underlying tool-use capabilities remain intact but obscured by formatting issues. The study explores various supervisory signals, such as off-policy supervision and hint-based guidance, applied through different training schemes to address these instabilities.

The researchers found that interleaving supervised fine-tuning with RL significantly improves training stability, though it may reduce performance when models face out-of-distribution formats and content. They also examined the effects of learning rates and generalization across different settings. These findings emphasize the importance of combining diverse supervisory signals with RL to enable robust training of LLMs for complex, multi-step tool-use tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26027v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool use enables large language models (LLMs) to perform complex tasks, and recent agentic reinforcement learning (RL) methods show promise for enhancing model capabilities. However, RL alone often leads to instability or limited gains in tool-use tasks. In our experiments, some models exhibit catastrophic collapse, where performance abruptly drops and tool-invocation structures fail. The analysis reveals that these failures stem from unexpected probability spikes in specific control tokens, disrupting structured execution, yet the underlying tool-use capability remains intact, merely obscured by specific formats. To address this, we systematically investigate a diverse set of supervisory signals, including off-policy supervision, hint-based guidance, erroneous example supervision, and others, applied under both synchronous and interleaved training schemes. We find that interleaving supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with RL substantially improves stability, but exhibits degraded performance under format and content out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation. We also analyze the impact of learning rates and generalization across settings. These results highlight the importance of understanding RL failures and demonstrate how diverse supervisory signals can guide exploratory learning, enabling robust training of LLMs for complex, multi-step tool-use tasks. items.title: Researchers audit 18 multimodal large language models for order sensitivity, finding 24-50% answer flip rates and limited mitigation from prompt changes [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Same Evidence, Different Answer: Auditing Order Sensitivity in Multimodal Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers conducted an audit of 18 leading multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to assess their sensitivity to the order of input data, a key reliability factor often overlooked in standard benchmarks. Using a new method called Facet-Probe, which examines five different facets of input ordering, they found that none of the models were order-invariant, with answer flip rates ranging from 24% to 50%. Even the best-performing model exhibited flips in 13.4% of trials, indicating significant variability in responses depending on input order.

The study employed a Bayesian item-response model to distinguish between noise and bias related to ordering and used controls to estimate baseline decoder variability. Attempts to mitigate order sensitivity through prompt modifications showed limited success and were modality-specific, failing to generalize from text to visual reasoning tasks. These findings suggest that prompt-level adjustments alone are insufficient for achieving robust order invariance, highlighting the need for future research into training methods and architectural changes. The authors propose adopting cross-ordering flip rate as a standard metric for evaluating MLLMs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26079v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standard benchmarks for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) score each item on one canonical ordering and miss whether order-irrelevant shuffling changes the answer, a baseline reliability property called for by emerging AI evaluation guidelines. We find that none of the 18 MLLMs we audit are order-invariant: screened per-facet panel-mean flip rates span 24-50%. A Gemini same-ordering control at temperature 0 estimates a substantial ordering excess over a same-input decoder-noise floor in verified cells. Capability predicts but does not eliminate flips; the best model still flips on 13.4% of trials. In our Gemini mitigation tests, training-free prompt changes are modality-conditional and do not transfer from text to visual reasoning. These results suggest that prompt-level mitigation alone is unlikely to provide general order robustness, motivating future work on training-time and architectural approaches. We propose cross-ordering flip rate as a standard reporting axis for MLLMs.

items.title: Researchers develop reinforcement learning-based adaptive sim-to-real alignment for vibration-based bearing health monitoring under data scarcity, achieving 92.8% accuracy across multiple testbeds [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Digital Twin-Driven Adaptive Sim-to-Real Alignment via Reinforcement Learning for Vibration-Based Bearing Health Monitoring Under Data Scarcity
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a reinforcement learning-based method to improve vibration-based bearing health monitoring under conditions of limited operational data. Their approach addresses the challenge of heterogeneous discrepancies between simulated and real-world signals by applying fault-type-specific feature alignment through a continuous-action Markov decision process. This method achieves a high accuracy of 92.8% across multiple testbeds without requiring encoder retraining, demonstrating effective and transferable fault diagnosis capabilities.

The technique uses Proximal Policy Optimization to learn adaptive affine corrections that balance minimizing the gap between simulated and real data while preserving the separability of different fault classes. An asymmetry-aware strategy reserves real data for normal conditions and augments fault data with aligned simulations. Validation on datasets from XJTU-SY, CWRU, and a custom slewing bearing testbed confirms the superiority of this reinforcement learning-driven alignment over traditional domain adaptation methods.
